#5451. Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

These models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

The popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

“Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” said Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

DevRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he said.

The ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.

Three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and users with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.

In September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.

Enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the big players.

“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin said.

Cost is currently the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.

“They are quickly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin said.

By most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.

“The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”

The pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.

In a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders said managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.

“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” said Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.

Experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” said Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.

Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, said open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.

“If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she said. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.

They’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., said in an interview with the Financial Times.

Sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing issue for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.

“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.

Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.

Advocates point to a shrinking capability gap, too, with some open-weight models nipping at the heels of the frontier alternatives. Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co., Ltd.’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks, according to Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute.

An agent built by Tenzai Inc. recently captured the top spot on HackerOne’s leaderboard using Z.ai Inc.’s GLM 5.2, generating 30% more findings per unit of computing power than a previous baseline using a proprietary model.

“What was the frontier 18 months ago is now well-mapped territory, and open-source models are closing the gap at a fraction of the cost” wrote Runware’s Hreninciuc.

Though such metrics explain open models’ ascendancy, the decision to use them isn’t open-and-shut. Experts cite four common myths that can mitigate the cost efficiencies.

One is the mistaken belief that open-weight models conflate with traditional open-source software and its permissive licenses. “This is a misnomer among many enterprises,” said Dr. Dorotea Baljević, EMEA Lead for AI Advisory at technology research and advisory firm Information Services Group. “There is licensing for these models in most cases, particularly for commercial usage.”

Although some, such as Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4, are covered by standard Apache or MIT licenses, terms and conditions vary. For example, Liquid AI Inc.’s open-weight models are free for commercial use only to organizations with less than $10 million in annual revenue.

“Other licenses require attribution, restrict certain application categories, or impose acceptable use policies, none of which carry a direct fee but all of which create legal exposure if ignored,” noted Bumu Technologies Inc., which does business as Nanobase.

Baljević said two hidden liabilities are data distribution rights for public training datasets used upstream and the evaluation, stability and legal audit costs that shift directly to the enterprise. “When using open-weight models, you need to lean in on understanding data distribution rights, copyright, contractual restrictions and consent,” she said. “In most cases, this carries costs.”

Evaluating models for accuracy, stability and explainability also falls to the user. With thousands of open-weight models available, the costs of a bake-off between multiple candidates can add up.

Baljević suggests organizations consider whether the model will be used internally or externally, the organization’s tolerance for accuracy, strategic fit and switching costs as evaluation criteria. Performance on public benchmarks also doesn’t guarantee a model will work well with an organization’s data, workflows and language.

Finance leaders may look at the 80% to 90% cost advantage of open-weight tokens and assume operational expenditures will drop proportionally. But tokens are only one part of the cost equation and not necessarily even the biggest one.

Organizations that plan to deploy models on their own infrastructure must bear the costs of integration, API development, IT infrastructure and human labor required for auditing and verification. A fraction of a cent saved on an inference call can be wiped out by the cost of a human expert spending a half-hour re-entering flawed database transactions.

Lack of visibility into how the model is operating can also produce sticker shock. A retry loop, in which an agent tries repeatedly to complete a failed task, can go on for hours or even days. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a case in which an AI-generated out-of-office message at a San Francisco-based software company went into a loop that ultimately burned $10,000 a day in token costs.

If a cheap open-weight model fails a multi-system query or generates invalid JSON, it triggers automated retries that can consume millions of secondary tokens. The human expertise required to repair the transaction manually can erase months of token savings.

“The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack is often the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities, APIs and such,” said Alex Bakker, an ISG distinguished analyst. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”

Using private graphics processing unit clusters eliminates external API fees, but self-hosting economics hinge on high, sustained utilization. Models that sit idle or at low usage levels consume power, create processing inefficiencies and incur costs if restarts are required.

Cast AI Group Inc. reported last spring that the average GPU utilization was 5% across thousands of clusters it monitored. Frontier models are usually a better option in that case. “Open models can be dramatically cheaper at high utilization, while frontier APIs remain cheaper for intermittent workloads because you aren’t paying for idle capacity,” said Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.

For intermittent workloads such as batch payroll processing or seasonal financial reporting, the organization pays 100% of capital expenses, power, cooling and depreciation while hardware idles.

“On-premises hosting wins when there is high, predictable 24/7 traffic where servers are constantly busy,” said Debojyoti Dutta, chief AI officer at Nutanix Inc. A hosted frontier model is a better choice “with spiky or lower traffic, where paying per token with zero setup cost is cheaper than renting idle hardware.”

When AI agents fail, the default reaction is to switch to a newer model, but benchmark data shows that approach is usually a dead end.

Most evaluation tests give agents relatively simple tasks and judge them mainly on whether they get the right answer. But real business environments are much more complicated. Agents must gather information from different systems, connect it correctly, handle growing amounts of data, and work within security rules.

This interface complexity is what usually breaks AI agents. DevRev estimates that moving an agent from clean test tools to real-world corporate use causes an 18% to 19% drop in accuracy. Upgrading the model improves performance by less than 1%.

“Every time a new model comes out, you need to re-evaluate your benchmarks, your models and your fine-tuning processes,” said Steven Yang, senior director of product management at Tanium Inc. That means better data integration is a more effective strategy than buying new models.

Though the open-weight option is viable for any company, experts say the best use cases are those where control, accountability and performance are paramount. The following three factors are at least as important as cost.

Compliance: Regulated industries have been held back from adopting AI over data residency and confidentiality concerns. Deploying open weights within enterprise data centers or virtual private clouds reduces the need for external data egress, ensures zero training data retention and allows for total physical isolation. The models also allow inspection of internal mechanics such as log-probabilities, token confidence scores and loss landscapes.

Training datasets, model weights and inference prompts never cross borders or leave the organization’s physical perimeter. That makes it easier to comply with strict data localization laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S. and the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe. Local auditing and observability also aid in compliance with regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires detailed logging, risk assessments and explainability.

But deploying on private infrastructure isn’t a cure-all. “You still have to maintain an aggressive data security posture around your processes because even open-weight models sometimes will take action trying to accomplish their tasks that could potentially violate some type of compliance rule,” said TEKSystems’ Franco.

Transparency: Understanding how models arrive at an answer is critical in many scenarios, particularly those involving safety, law and finance. “Open-weight models expose the math behind their answers,” said Brian Weiss, chief technology officer at document processing platform maker Hyperscience, the business name of Hyper Labs Inc. “You can use that to hold the model accountable for accuracy.”

In contrast, frontier APIs often obscure the equations used to generate probabilities, which are critical to assessing accuracy. Asking a model how confident it is in its answer may yield a subjective response. Open weights allow confidence scores to be scored against ground-truth outcomes for better reliability.

“People can take these models inside their organization, do some post-training and fine-tuning and have a customized model where they know the costs, where it’s sitting and what data is being sent to it,” said David DeSanto, CEO of Anaconda Inc., maker of an AI development platform.

“The future is an orchestrated ensemble of bounded, transparent, governed, cost-effective models,” Weiss said. “If I find a better model for a particular task, I can swap it out because I have the framework to do that.”

Performance: As organizations move from the relatively simple generative AI question-and-response metaphor to sophisticated multi-agent frameworks, latency issues can compound exponentially. For example, a 500-millisecond API delay across 50 sequential reasoning steps creates 25 seconds of cumulative latency, which would render many applications useless.

Executing open-weight models directly alongside operational databases or within containerized edge pods minimizes routing hops and rate limits. Distillation, which trains smaller, specialized open models from frontier “teacher” models, is faster.

Hyperscience reported that distillation delivers up to 97% cost reduction and four times faster inference, while retaining over 95% of the original model’s performance on designated tasks. Small models are faster and considerably cheaper than frontier LLMs.

Experts say constructing a business case for open-weight models requires understanding three major sources of hidden expense.

Complexity tax: Reasoning can break down when open-weight models interact with complex enterprise data at scale. The “Cartesian Shortcut” refers to a phenomenon in which AI models rely on workarounds learned during training rather than demonstrating a flexible understanding of the problem they’re trying to solve.

Google LLC researchers found that the models struggled with visual reasoning problems, such as solving mazes, when the data was presented in a circular rather than a grid layout. Leading models answered 69% to 83% of the square-grid problems correctly, but their accuracy fell to below 40% when the problems appeared in circular layouts.

The corollary to a business scenario is a multihop join across multiple systems. Models may “cheat” by collapsing field-level relationships into hierarchical groupings, generating massive data fabrications.

Human oversight remains critical: “For validation and rework, humans in the loop need to be taken into account on top of all the tokens you’re paying for already,” said TekSystems’ Franco.

Poor data quality: Foundation models can’t fix bad data, a fact that’s holding back AI adoption across the board. The Hyperscience/Harris Poll study found that 86% of IT leaders said dirty internal data is actively crippling GenAI performance.

Feeding error-strewn or outdated information into probabilistic models creates “context pollution,” the accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, outdated or contradictory information. When agents execute multistep database joins, system workflows or automated tool calls based on flawed data or ambiguous schemas, cascading errors can occur.

Sauce Labs Inc. Chief Technology Officer Anoop Tripathi recommends creating validated “golden datasets” for fine-tuning and evaluation. He also cautions architects against misapplying probabilistic AI to structured business logic. In other words, use models only where they add value and apply conventional (and cheaper) data processing to everything else.

Continuous evaluation: Selecting the right model out of thousands of open-weight alternatives requires ongoing evaluation against internal workloads rather than public leaderboards. That demands expensive MLOps, site reliability engineering and platform engineering skills.

Because new models are constantly being introduced and revised, Circuit & Chisel’s Amira recommends building custom testing harnesses that can quickly evaluate candidate models against business-relevant tasks.

Rather than treating open-weight adoption as an all-or-nothing choice, enterprise architects should bucket organizational tasks into distinct operational tiers. Don’t feed every problem into a token-hungry trillion-parameter model if a smaller, specialized one will do the trick.

“Organizations don’t give a heavyweight reasoning model a lightweight sorting job,” said Nutanix’s Dutta. “They divide their business workloads into tiers based on cost, speed and hardware footprint.”

Lower-tier workloads such as search, embeddings and document classification work well with inexpensive, compact open-weight and small language models. Sophisticated tasks such as autonomous reasoning and restructuring large, deeply entangled legacy software systems are better suited to commercial alternatives.

ISG’s Bakker believes the need for constant evaluation is the biggest impediment to open-weight adoption. “The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack will likely be the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities and APIs,” he said. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”

Enterprise IT organizations must develop expertise in local model execution, containerized execution sandboxes and agent harness orchestration. Managing AI and agents safely “is, in the near future, going to be as important an indigenous knowledge as how to upgrade Windows,” said Gordon Allott, founder and CEO of private infrastructure provider nFOX Lab.

The shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management. Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task. That’s a discipline that was barely on the roadmap a year ago.

At the start of the year, there was no way enterprises were going to touch open-weight models, Brad Maltz, head of AI factory solutions at Dell Technologies Inc., said in a November interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE’s streaming media platform. “People were pretty wrong about that. I think the open-weight movement is the future.”

#5450. Bronwyn Newport Gives Estranged Husband Todd Bradley a Tour of Her New Salt Lake City Home: ‘It’s Time To Move On’

Bronwyn Newport has a new Utah home—and she just gave fans and her estranged husband a tour of the dwelling.

On the Nov. 25 episode of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City,” the fashion blogger received a visit from Todd Bradley, her estranged husband. The couple announced their separation in December 2025 after nine years of marriage.

The tech investor initially said he “just wanted to come by and see” Newport and her new home, but soon admitted that he had stopped by to apologize after an explosive conversation the pair had shared over dinner in the previous episode.

In a confessional interview, Newport admitted that Bradley had reached out to smooth things over after their last dramatic conversation, but that she had not yet been ready to talk.

Instead, she extended an invitation to her new property.

“I invited him to the house because it’s a smaller, nicer way for me to say, ‘This is what I’m doing, and this is the direction I’m going,’ without saying things that are hard for him to hear,” she explained.

Bradley had not yet seen the home in person, although he said it looked nice in the photographs he had looked at. Newport offered him a tour of “some of it.”

“The whole basement is going to be Gwen and Logan’s domain,” she explained, referring to her 20-year-old daughter and her daughter’s boyfriend.

The ground level of the home—which was empty at the time of the impromptu tour—featured hardwood flooring, an open-concept plan, a fireplace, and plenty of windows. There were also recessed lights and a glass sliding door, which led to an outdoor space.

“Upstairs is really Muzzy’s space,” Newport said as she walked up the steps of the yet-to-be-furnished home with Bradley.

She said that the upstairs space—in which her mother, who goes by Muzzy, will reside in—includes a kitchen and essentially functions as an apartment.

Finally, Newport brought Bradley into her primary squite, a light-filled space lined with expansive windows. The room features an en suite bathroom with a walk-in shower and tub, which she said she’s very excited about, as she and Bradley had previously discussed a remodel of the home they shared, which would have included a lavish bathtub.

There’s also a well-organized walk-in closet, though fans of the show will understand that it’s likely not going to be enough space for Newport’s massive wardrobe.

In a Sept. 30 interview with Vulture, she did a photo shoot in a storage unit she has in the nearby suburb of Millcreek, UT, which serves the sole purpose of storing all of her clothes and accessories.

“It’s very weird to give Todd a tour of a house that’s going to be mine and not his,” she said during the episode. “There is a part of me that feels I need to be totally free and separate of Todd, but there’s a part of me that is scared to death to not have Todd be a part of my life at all.”

Newport and Bradley had moved into a sprawling Salt Lake City home not long before she joined the cast. In a September 2024 tour of the previous abode, she said they had been living there for a year and a half after moving from nearby Park City.

In the video, Newport revealed she came across the home in a viral listing. It had originally featured a sunken floor with a "psychedelic carpet,” which she said she “liked and really wanted to keep.”

Per Bradley’s wishes, they upgraded the space to have sleek hardwood floors.

“I love a project, so I wanted this old, haunted house in Salt Lake that we could remodel,” she said. “When we first came in, I was obsessed with this living room, the view of Salt Lake and the mountains, all the light, and a big space for me to have tons of parties all of the time.”

The home was boldly decorated, with a royal blue kitchen, rainbow couches in the living room, and a color-drenched lavender office space, with built-in shelving filled with art and designer accessories.

After their separation, Newport and Bradley sold the home for an undisclosed amount in an off-market deal.

The transaction has become a storyline this season of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City,” with friend of the cast Britani Bateman flexing her real estate expertise to suggest that the home was priced too high when it was on the market, and that Newport must not have received the 50-50 split from the sale that she had claimed to get.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5449. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

#5448. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Fully Connected event

AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.

As inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs. The emergence of continuously learning agents and physical AI applications is further complicating that equation. For CoreWeave Inc., the changing workload mix is altering the economics of infrastructure delivery, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier.

“What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante said. “They’ve got networking; they’ve got storage. They’ve got this software layer, which is observability. They’ve got security in there. They’ve got this closed-loop system between evaluation, observation [and] runtime curating … that’s sort of how they’re saying their software layer is now intact.”

During the Fully Connected event, Vellante and Furrier spoke with CoreWeave executives, technology partners and customers about the technical and economic realities of running artificial intelligence at production scale. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video analysis with Dave Vellante and John Furrier:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s exclusive coverage of this event:

The commercial value of inference depends on both token volume and delivery speed. Nvidia Corp.’s Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, which works with its Vera Rubin platform, is attracting interest in financial technology and other sectors that require real-time processing, according to Ian Buck, vice president and general manager of hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia.

“Data centers have a natural cap, and that cap is actually their power,” he told theCUBE. “With every generation of GPU, we make sure that our tokens per watt is upwards of 10 times more efficient. In fact, we saw that with Blackwell — we got, in the end, a 30x improvement in tokens per watt.”

Memory management adds another dimension to AI infrastructure economics as agents engage in increasingly lengthy interactions. A single session involving 500,000 tokens can consume between 5% and 10% of a graphics processing unit’s memory. Retaining session context in persistent storage can reduce costly recalculations, according to Alon Horev, co-founder and chief technology officer of Vast Data Inc.

“You can move a session from one busy GPU to one less busy GPU and move KV cache either over the network or read it from Vast,” he told theCUBE. “Once you look at inference as a distributed problem where you have the opportunity to use GPU memory, CPU memory and Vast across a fleet of machines, you have more optionality and you have more optimized scheduling.”

For AI-native startups, specialized cloud providers offer an alternative to owning capital-intensive infrastructure. LlamaIndex Inc. processes millions of document pages daily for customers in finance, legal services and insurance. Inference accounts for about 75% of its workloads, with training accounting for the remainder, according to Jerry Liu, co-founder and chief executive officer of LlamaIndex.

“We serve a lot of different customers at extremely persistent and also spiky workloads,” he told theCUBE. “We really, really need to make sure that we have the right capacity to serve our customers without getting throttled.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Ian Buck:

Protecting AI infrastructure investments starts on the factory floor. Dell Technologies Inc. has developed modular rack designs to accommodate different power and cooling configurations. Its collaboration with CoreWeave includes integrating the cloud provider’s Racky management software into factory testing and improving liquid-cooling leak detection, according to Sarat Krishnan, director of PowerEdge AI architecture and systems development engineering at Dell.

“It becomes increasingly expensive to remediate and fix something as you go later on in the manufacturing process; [it] becomes extremely expensive if you have to replace something in the data center,” he told theCUBE. “What we have done over the last two years is shift our most complex diagnostics — the ones that are going to capture true hardware failures — further and further left.”

At Cognition AI Inc., continuous model improvement involves training across data centers in multiple countries. The company’s Devin software engineering agent now handles tasks ranging from code development to resolving production issues, according to Chen Goldberg (pictured, left), executive vice president of product and engineering at CoreWeave, and Silas Alberti (right), head of research and founding team at Cognition. To support these learning systems, CoreWeave introduced Forge, a platform that connects inference, evaluation and model refinement and incorporates Agent Lens to trace agent activity.

“If you run a big training run, you’re not just looking at the GPUs, but you also want uptime,” Alberti said during the event. “If just one replica goes down, the whole training run goes down. I think a very important metric is getting to this 99.99% reliability.”

For International Business Machines Corp., the power and cooling demands of newer hardware helped drive its decision to work with CoreWeave. The relationship has since expanded to include joint engineering around identity management and workload isolation through CoreWeave Sandboxes. IBM also benchmarks the performance impact of security controls to inform architectural decisions, according to Brian Belgodere, senior technical staff member at IBM.

“This is a supply chain problem, top to bottom,” Belgodere told theCUBE. “It’s not just the hardware: it’s the firmware, kernel levels, code, your data provenance. Then you get into the whole world of agents, your images. It is an absolute provenance problem.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Brian Belgodere:

For organizations deploying physical AI, implementation time is a key consideration in AI infrastructure economics. Aston Martin F1, whose race cars generate a million data points per second each, operates under strict budget constraints and development deadlines. CoreWeave’s forward-deployed engineering approach brings specialized expertise to those operations, according to Richard Ahlfeld, senior vice president of physical AI at CoreWeave, and Eric Ernst, commercial technology ambassador of AMR GP Ltd., trading as Aston Martin F1.

“We really need people that can be outside of the car development phase and come in with the fresh knowledge of what’s happening in this industry that is moving extremely quickly,” Ernst said during the event. “You can build as many processes as you want, call it agile, whatever you want. You cannot stop that process. You got to hit a deadline.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Richard Ahlfeld and Eric Ernst:

Walden Robotics Inc. uses large-scale virtual simulation to prepare robots for physical deployment. Its robots have been working full production shifts alongside humans since May, performing tasks such as machine tending, parts kitting and subassembly, according to Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics, and John Mancuso, vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc.

“If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon told theCUBE. “We do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”

Here’s theCUBE’s full video discussion with John Mancuso and Adrien Gaidon:

#5446. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”

#5445. AI infrastructure stocks continue their slide, but Anthropic closes higher

Investors continued to offload artificial intelligence infrastructure stocks today, but Anthropic PBC recouped some of its losses from earlier this week.

The AI selloff reportedly began in August. It accelerated on Nov. 17, the day Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang resigned over his affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a cloud provider under investigation over alleged export control violations. Huang returned to the helm of the chipmaker Monday.

Nvidia closed at $173.73 the day before Huang’s resignation. It dropped as low as $125 during the executive’s two-week hiatus and surged 30% on Monday, the day he returned. Nvidia lost some of its recent gains in today’s trading session: Its share price closed 3.8% lower.

Other AI chip stocks have also taken a hit. Broadcom Inc. closed a small fraction of a percent lower than yesterday, while Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. fell 1.6% and 0.6%, respectively.

The semiconductor stock that logged the biggest drop today is Ambarella Inc., a relatively low-profile maker of AI image analysis chips. Its accelerators are used by edge devices to process footage from their cameras. Ambarella dropped 19.8% today after closing 19% lower yesterday.

The stock’s decline was driven not so much by the broader AI selloff, but rather the weak earnings that Ambarella posted on Tuesday. The company missed expectations across the board. Ambarella said that some customers had canceled or delayed orders to mitigate the financial impact of soaring memory prices.

Micron Inc., one of the world’s top memory chip suppliers, saw its market capitalization drop more than 4.5% today. That’s despite CEO Sanjay Mehrotra’s recent disclosure that the company has already sold out 75% of its 2027 manufacturing capacity. According to the executive, the gap between memory demand and supply is only set to increase next year.

Companies downstream from chipmakers in the AI data center supply chain fared better. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. ended the trading session 1.8% higher after dipping into the red earlier today, while Dell Technologies Inc. gained 0.64%.

In contrast, the major cloud providers weren’t left out of today’s selloff. Amazon.com Inc., the cloud market’s largest player, closed 3% lower. Microsoft Corp. and Google LLC dropped 1.25% and 2%, respectively. Oracle Corp., which trails the three companies in market share but has emerged as an important AI infrastructure provider, took the biggest hit: It’s down 5% from yesterday.

Anthropic ended the trading session with a 1% gain. The company thereby recouped some of yesterday’s losses, which pushed its stock below its $80 debut price. Anthropic went public last week through a record-setting offering that raised more than $93 billion.

Overall, the tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 0.6% while the S&P 500 slid 0.25%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 0.33%.

#5444. NAR’s latest data, must-have AI tools, Compass’ 15 new lawsuits

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

#5443. Attacker used 1Password employee’s GitHub account to copy customer records

Identity security company 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker, working through an employee’s corporate GitHub account, copied account records belonging to a subset of its customers.

According to the company, the incident came to light on Nov. 19, when 1Password began investigating signs that the GitHub account had been compromised. Using the account, the attacker is said to have pushed malicious code to 1Password’s backend services, which then downloaded what the company describes as “administrative data pertaining to our customers.”

The records taken include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters and other non-secret account metadata. Rounding out the list are tokens found in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery.

Customer vaults, the items stored in them and the keys that protect them were not affected, according to 1Password. “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” the company said in its disclosure. Account passwords and Secret Keys are not stored by the company. Also left untouched, the company says, were account recovery keys and the 1Password apps and browser extensions.

Beyond the customer records, the attacker is said to have copied source code from private repositories. Access was also gained to 1Password’s continuous integration and continuous delivery system, which contains infrastructure-related secrets needed for its product to work. According to 1Password, the source code contains no user secrets. Having triggered a rotation of all credentials that may have been exposed, the company claims there has been no impact to its services, availability or product security.

The tokens taken from emailed links cannot be used on their own to access an account, since completing an invitation or recovery also requires a sign-in through single sign-on or a six-digit code sent to the user’s registered email address. Users with provisioning invites or recovery requests pending at the time of the incident, said to be a small number, have been notified directly.

As a precaution, the emailed codes have now been lengthened from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters. 1Password says it has found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed tokens. Other steps taken in response include disabling the affected GitHub account, revoking the stolen token, tightening internal controls and bringing in independent cybersecurity experts to validate its containment and remediation work.

Customers do not need to change anything in their 1Password accounts. The company is instead warning users to be cautious of phishing attempts, such as unexpected emails, texts or calls about invitations or account recovery requests they did not start. “1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key,” the company noted.

1Password, which claims to serve more than 200,000 businesses, did not say how many customers had records downloaded. How the employee’s GitHub account was compromised was also left unexplained.

This is not the first intrusion 1Password has disclosed. In October 2023, the company said that an attacker had accessed its Okta tenant using session data stolen in the breach of Okta Inc.’s customer support system. No user data was found to have been compromised in that case.

Today’s disclosure comes nearly four years after rival password manager LastPass US LP revealed that a hacker had copied encrypted customer password vaults, using information taken in an earlier breach of its development environment.

1Password says it will update its post if the investigation turns up anything that changes what it has disclosed so far.

#5442. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5439. FCC clears SpaceX to put up to 1 million Starmind data centers in space

Elon Musk’s Space Exploration Technologies Corp. today received approval from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to operate as data centers in orbit.

Issued by the FCC’s Space Bureau under delegated authority, the order is described by the agency as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space.”

“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.”

Replying to Carr on X, Musk wrote that Starmind “will be a great asset to America and the world.”

Under the terms of the approval, the Starmind satellites are to sit in six orbital shells, or altitude bands, between 500 and 1,002 kilometers, below the 2,000-kilometer ceiling in SpaceX’s original application. Most communications will run over optical links to other satellites, including those in the Starlink network. The license itself covers a backup Ka-band radio system for emergency telemetry, tracking and command.

The approval does come with conditions. SpaceX’s orbital debris plan was found to comply with the agency’s rules only for satellites below 600 kilometers, and four of the six shells sit above that line. Before deploying anything higher, SpaceX is required to file a modification application containing a final debris plan.

A request from the company to retire some of those higher satellites into disposal orbits around Earth or the sun, rather than having them re-enter the atmosphere within five years, was deferred for lack of information.

To keep the authorization, SpaceX has to have its first Starmind satellite in operation by Nov. 25, 2033. The schedule then calls for 100,000 satellites by 2035, 500,000 by 2038 and the full 1 million by 2040. Missing any of the deadlines would void the license.

Petitions to deny the application from Amazon.com Inc.’s Amazon Leo satellite business, Viasat Inc. and the American Astronomical Society were all rejected. In a March filing, Amazon had described the plan as “a lofty ambition rather than a real plan.”

According to the bureau, nothing in the FCC’s rules limits how many satellites a single constellation can include. Astronomers’ concerns about the satellites’ brightness in infrared were ruled to fall outside the scope of a radio license.

SpaceX first applied for the system in January, shortly before it acquired Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI Corp. Orbital data centers then featured in SpaceX’s pitch to investors ahead of its record initial public offering in June. Built around a space-optimized version of Nvidia Corp.’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system, the first-generation Starmind satellite, known as AI1, could reach orbit as early as the third quarter of next year, according to Musk.

The competitors Carr referred to include Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin LLC, which applied in March for Project Sunrise, a planned network of up to 51,600 data center satellites. Starcloud Inc., a startup developing AI data centers in orbit, raised $250 million at a $2.3 billion valuation in August.

#5434. US intelligence agencies reportedly brief Congress about Alice Huang

U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly briefed Congressional staffers about Alice Huang, the cloud executive at the center of the Jensen Huang controversy.

The classified discussion took place on Tuesday, sources told the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal today. It was attended by staff members of the House and Senate intelligence committees. The briefing is said to have included representatives of the FBI, CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

Alice Huang is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean cloud provider that has reportedly bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia Corp. chips. The company is under investigation for allegedly breaching U.S. export controls. Those controls prohibit companies from selling cutting-edge artificial intelligence chips to customers in China.

On Oct. 29, the Times revealed that Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang. The paper stated that she had been “found to be passing intelligence” to China. A few days later, other outlets reported that U.S. officials had not yet concluded that Alice Huang is a spy. The U.S. Justice Department reaffirmed that’s the case shortly thereafter.

According to the Times, this week’s classified Congressional briefing included a summary of the information that U.S. intelligence agencies have collected about Alice Huang. Those agencies’ representatives reportedly “did not dispute” that she had gathered information for China. However, they stated that there’s no evidence China’s MSS spy agency directed her to initiate the affair.

Some U.S. officials reportedly believe Alice Huang can still be considered a spy. Others are said to see her ties to the country’s intelligence service as ”more circumstantial.” According to the Journal, officials don’t believe that Alice Huang passed any “intelligence of significance” to China.

The briefers reportedly told Congressional staffers that Kang Wei, a businessman believed to be Huang’s husband, is a “more significant” figure. They stated that Kang is a Chinese intelligence asset who was “often” in touch with the country’s spy agency.

On Nov. 12, the Journal reported that Kang had known Jensen Huang for over a decade. The publication later revealed that he had built a data center network in China.

The briefing reportedly did not cover the most sensitive information the U.S. intelligence community has gathered about Alice Huang. Additionally, it didn’t include a classified memo about her relationship with Jensen Huang that was drafted under the supervision of U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio. Congressional staffers requested a copy of the memo.

Jensen Huang is set to appear before three House committees on Dec. 1. Prior to the spy controversy, he was reportedly scheduled to make a product announcement that day. The closed-door briefing will be followed by a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

#5432. 5 Interesting Startup Deals You May Have Missed: Reflecting Sunlight From Space, Better Breathing And Smarter Garbage Trucks

This is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here.

What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth? Or researchers could send an experiment into space for less than the price of a car?

Those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month. Our latest roundup also includes a company bringing AI to the old-school business of garbage hauling, another rethinking how factories are programmed, and a consumer brand betting that better breathing could become a big business. Let’s take a closer look.

Solar power has one rather obvious limitation: The sun goes down.

To that end, Reflect Orbital is working on a solution that sounds straight out of science fiction. The Hawthorne, California-based startup wants to put giant mirrors in orbit to redirect sunlight toward specific locations on Earth, potentially allowing solar farms to keep generating electricity longer after sunset.

The company recently announced $73.5 million in new funding, bringing its total funding to more than $102 million, per Crunchbase. Existing investors Sequoia Capital, Lux Capital and Starship Ventures participated, alongside new backers including Buckley Ventures, Convective Capital, The Uncommon Group and Salesforce Ventures 1.

Reflect Orbital is developing lightweight, foldable reflectors that it says can be launched aboard satellites and deployed in low Earth orbit. The company envisions using them not only to extend solar power generation, but also to illuminate disaster zones for nighttime search-and-rescue operations or construction sites after dark.

The idea remains unproven in orbit, however. Reflect Orbital is targeting the second quarter of 2027 for its first demonstration mission, which has received FCC approval. The funding will help support those initial launches, further development of its reflector technology, and commercial partnerships.

The raise comes during a record year for space technology funding. By late August, investors had poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally, per Crunchbase data, already comfortably exceeding previous annual records.

Nasal strips have been around for decades, but Intake Breathing Technology thinks there’s room for a serious upgrade.

The Santa Barbara, California-based consumer wellness company recently announced a $62 million investment from Camino Partners, the investment platform founded by KIND Snacks entrepreneur Daniel Lubetzky.

Intake makes a patented magnetic nasal dilator designed to open nasal passages and improve airflow. Rather than relying on a conventional adhesive strip stretched across the nose, its system uses adhesive tabs and a reusable magnetic band to pull the sides of the nose outward.

The company markets its product to people looking to breathe more comfortably while sleeping, exercising or going about their daily routines. It says it has sold more than 100 million pairs of breathing tabs since 2023, with triple-digit revenue growth over the past three years.

Intake plans to use the new capital to expand beyond its direct-to-consumer business and into more mainstream retail channels. That’s where Lubetzky’s experience building KIND into a household name could prove useful.

Its funding comes as venture investors show renewed enthusiasm for fitness and wellness. Startups in those categories raised more than $3.6 billion globally in the first half of 2026, putting the sector on pace for its strongest funding year since 2022, Crunchbase data shows.

Interestingly, much of this year’s investment into the sector has flowed to wearable devices and health platforms built around AI and data. Intake is a somewhat different bet: a relatively simple physical product that has apparently found a sizable audience without promising to reinvent healthcare through software.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Fitness- And Wellness-Related Startup Funding In 2026

Taking out the trash isn’t exactly rocket science. But managing the businesses that collect it turns out to be surprisingly complicated.

San Francisco-based TrashLab Software recently raised $12 million in a growth funding round led by Ventana, with participation from existing investors Bienville Capital, Harlem Capital and CreativeCo.

The startup builds an AI-powered operating platform for waste-hauling businesses, an industry where many smaller operators still rely on spreadsheets, paper routes and clunky software to manage their fleets.

TrashLab says its platform combines dispatching, route planning, customer management, billing and payments. Its AI agent, called Haul-E, can answer customer calls and take orders, while cameras in garbage trucks can help document problems such as overflowing dumpsters, blocked containers or bins that weren’t put out for collection.

The company says hundreds of waste haulers across the U.S. and Canada now use its software, and that more than 5 million tons of material have been managed through its platform.

It’s not the only startup finding an AI opportunity in the waste industry. We recently covered Greyparrot, a London-based company using computer vision to identify and analyze waste moving through recycling facilities. While Greyparrot focuses on what happens after trash reaches a processing plant, TrashLab is tackling the messy logistics of getting it there.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To Waste Management Startups In 2026

Factory automation has come a long way, but programming the machines that run industrial production lines can still require specialized expertise and a lot of time.

Gardena, California-based Neuron Industries wants to make the process a lot simpler.

The startup recently announced a $10 million seed round co-led by FCVC and Obvious Ventures, with participation from Y Combinator, Thin Line Capital, Zee Prime Capital and Founder Factor.

Neuron is developing a new kind of industrial controller — the hardware that coordinates sensors, motors and other equipment in factories — alongside AI-powered software that lets engineers describe what they want a machine to do in ordinary language.

Its system generates control code that engineers can inspect, modify and test in simulation before deploying it to real equipment. The goal is to reduce the time and specialized programming knowledge needed to get new production lines up and running.

The startup says it has already demonstrated its technology on existing factory equipment, including replacing an aging controller on a wood-processing line with roughly three hours of engineering work and eight hours of downtime. It plans to release its Cortex AI Controller commercially in early 2027.

The investment fits into a broader surge in funding for physical AI — technology that applies artificial intelligence to robots, autonomous vehicles, industrial equipment and other machines in the real world. Startups in those categories raised $47.4 billion globally across 521 deals in the first half of 2026, nearly 4x the amount invested in the second half of 2025, according to Crunchbase data.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Physical AI Venture Funding In 2026

Sending an experiment into space has traditionally required years of preparation, specialized engineering expertise and a very substantial budget.

Austria-based Tumbleweed wants to bring the cost of entry down to as little as 15,000 euros.

The Vienna startup recently raised 6.9 million euros (roughly $8 million) in seed funding led by PactVC, with participation from Vanagon Ventures, Prototype Capital and EWOR, among other investors. The company describes it as the largest space-tech seed round raised in Austria to date.

Tumbleweed develops standardized containers, called Pods, that allow researchers and companies to conduct experiments in microgravity without building their own satellites or navigating the complex certification process required for space missions.

Customers can place their experiments inside the pre-certified containers, which provide power and communications capabilities while in orbit. The startup handles the logistics of launching the payloads and transmitting experimental data back to Earth.

Unlike many space startups still working toward their first launch, Tumbleweed has already put hardware in orbit. Its inaugural Oasis Alpha satellite launched in July carrying experiments for four paying customers, including research into biological processes and space-resource technologies. The mission was fully booked a year before launch.

Tumbleweed says its new funding will help it carry out three more missions in 2027 and develop a next-generation spacecraft that would allow customers to bring physical samples back to Earth beginning in 2028.

Tumbleweed is part of a growing European space startup ecosystem, although funding remains concentrated elsewhere. As of late August, European companies had attracted about 10% of global space-tech venture investment in 2026, compared with the more than 60% going to U.S. startups, Crunchbase data shows.

Related Crunchbase query: Space And Satellite Tech Startup Funding
