#5385. Microsoft ‘To Do’ users make a big to-do over popular task app’s pending retirement

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:07 pm

Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now they’re being asked to pack up again.

Microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The company said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft announced Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist users may end up back with the people who built it.

#5384. Holiday shoppers let AI agents find gifts — but don't trust them with their credit cards

Walmart, Shopify and Meta have built ways for AI agents to pay. By default, those tools still need the shopper's okay on each order before money moves

Amando Komoda runs a Minneapolis company that sells supplies for dry-aging meat, and he uses an AI agent called Instinct to set up alerts for hard-to-find parts, such as a particular Raspberry Pi chip, so he doesn't have to search for them himself. Often he still buys the part himself. When he does let Instinct pay, he approves the purchase first and gives the agent a credit card number that works only once, so it can't charge anything he hasn't agreed to. "I wouldn't give it access to my best credit card," he told Business Insider. "I've watched enough sci-fi movies that I can't trust it completely."

Komoda's caution is the opposite of what Meta $META and OpenAI promised when they launched their agents this fall. Meta and OpenAI pitched agents that would shop day and night and find the cheapest option without their owners having to check. Millions of people signed up. Meta said on Oct. 21 that more than 10 million people had set up Muse, the agent it launched in September.

Far fewer have let their agents pay. Just 12% of U.S. shoppers, about one in eight, say they've let their own AI agent buy something for them, according to a holiday survey that Salesforce $CRM, the business software company, published Nov. 12. Shoppers don't trust AI agents to spend their money yet, and Meta can't earn much from Muse until people let it complete their purchases.

Loni Stark, Adobe $ADBE's vice president of strategy and product, has built two AI agents herself and expects tools like them to take over the part of shopping people dread. "We don't like the anxiety of wondering whether we got the best price or not," she told Business Insider. "We're going to offload that to agents." She still decides when her agents spend her money. Museli, the agent she built on Muse, handled an entire purchase of ballet shoes from Nordstrom $JWN's website, but it got her permission before it paid. Her other agent, Molty, researches products she's thinking about buying, and she has never connected it to a way to pay.

People can approve every payment themselves and still end up paying with the wrong card. Katie Notopoulos, a senior correspondent at Business Insider, asked Muse to order her a salad while she was reviewing three agents. Muse offered her a debit card or a Mastercard $MA from the accounts she had already linked. She picked the Mastercard because she didn't recognize its last four digits and assumed it was the new credit card that had just come in the mail. When she checked her wallet, she found she had chosen her health savings account card, which works only for medical expenses. She was so busy sorting out the mix-up that she never told Muse to place the order, and Muse never sent it. "This turned out to be a real fiasco," she wrote, "and I learned my lesson: it would have been infinitely easier for me to just do it myself.

Like Notopoulos, most U.S. holiday shoppers still want to handle their own payments, even when AI does the searching. About two in five U.S. shoppers now rely mainly on generative AI for at least one holiday task, the consulting firm Deloitte's annual holiday survey found, yet fewer than half of them would trust the tool to complete a purchase, even with their permission. Nearly twice as many people would trust an AI agent to pick gifts for friends and family as would let it pay with their card, even if they could check its work first, a September survey by the customer-service software company Talkdesk found. Shoppers are ready to let an agent find the gift but not to let it spend their money.

Muse users do buy things. More than a quarter of Muse's weekly users shop with it, Meta told analysts on its Oct. 21 earnings call. In Muse's first week, people bought so much more than anyone expected that Meta had to work with the payments company Stripe to raise credit limits.

Across the web, though, agents mostly browse. HUMAN Security, which sells software that spots and blocks bots, found that AI agent traffic on the sites it protects grew about eightfold from August to October, and most of it landed on shopping sites. Nearly all of the agent visits were for browsing. Most went to product and search pages, and fewer than one in 50 reached a checkout or payment page. HUMAN counts where a request lands, not whether anyone bought anything, so even a visit to a checkout page doesn't prove a sale.

Many of the sites HUMAN protects keep Muse out entirely. Blocked agent requests hit a record in September, and HUMAN said Muse was the main reason. The company's fraud software blocks Muse unless a site chooses to allow it, and because the agent is so new, many sites still haven't. Susan J. Li, a Meta executive, told analysts on the earnings call that some businesses are "understandably focused on protecting customer relationships." On sites that block Muse, the agent can't buy anything, and its users have to shop for themselves.

Even where agents get in, the puzzles and texted login codes that stores use to confirm a person is buying can stop them before they pay. Komoda, the Minneapolis business owner, often finishes purchases himself because Instinct can't always solve the Captcha puzzles some checkouts require. When Business Insider reporter Notopoulos had OpenAI's agent, Dot, get her lunch, Dot kept getting stuck on the six-digit login code sent to her phone, and she had to request the code three times before the order went through.

Walmart $WMT and Shopify $SHOP have built checkouts for agents, and both keep a person in charge of every purchase. Walmart announced on Oct. 21 that each AI agent would get a profile of its own inside a customer's account, under a system the company calls Agent Profiles. By default, the agent has to ask for approval before it buys anything. People can instead let it buy on its own up to a limit they set, such as $50, and the agent never sees their card number.

Shopify asks people to approve every payment an agent makes at its merchants' stores. Shopify's checkout inside Meta's AI services, Muse among them, is switched on by default for eligible stores, and it covers buyers in 11 countries, including the U.S. In every purchase Shopify describes, people review the order and approve the payment before it goes through.

Meta's plan to make money from Muse depends on how often people approve a purchase. On the earnings call, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Meta would start making money from Muse sooner than it usually does with a new product, under a model in which it collects "a percent of the value that we are helping to create for people." But Meta collects its percentage only on the sales people let Muse finish. Li, the Meta executive, told analysts that the company expects many Muse experiences to "remain AI assisted rather than fully autonomous" in the near term.

Once Meta collects a share of each sale, people have one more reason to check the price and the seller before they say yes. Shoppers already worry about AI pushing them toward the wrong purchase. Nearly three in four people in Talkdesk's survey want stronger rules on how retailers use AI, and 40% worry they could be misled into buying something that isn't right for them.

This Cyber Monday, many shoppers will send agents to find gifts but still read the price, check who's selling, and type in their own card numbers. The agents save them the search. Checking out is still a job people do themselves.

#5383. Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company says it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report says.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the company says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5382. Dow rallies nearly 600 points to close out its best week since 2022

The S&P 500 gained more than 5% and the Nasdaq more than 6% for the week, which ended with an early close

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 591.99 points, or 1.2%, to close at 50,774.94 on Friday. That was the index's steepest one-week climb since October 2022, according to CNBC.

The S&P 500 climbed 1.6%, settling at 7,297.49, and a 2.3% rise lifted the Nasdaq $NDAQ Composite to 24,129.50. U.S. markets were closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and shut at 1 p.m. ET on Friday.

Technology stocks led the rebound. Meta $META Platforms stock rose more than 3%, Amazon $AMZN stock gained about 4% and Broadcom $AVGO stock climbed close to 4%.

For the week, the Dow and the S&P 500 each gained more than 5%, and the Nasdaq gained more than 6%. The S&P 500 turned in its strongest week since April 2025, and the Nasdaq posted its largest weekly gain since April, according to CNBC.

The week began with Nvidia $NVDA reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. Nvidia stock jumped 31% on Monday, and the Dow gained over 1,400 points, or 3%. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq each logged their strongest one-day performance since April 2025 on Monday, according to CNBC.

#5381. Trump has found something to blame for his midterm loss: ‘Fake’ growth numbers out of Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department

The headaches just keep piling up for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been on his case about the Commerce Department’s handling of Nvidia, following the news of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. And now President Trump is blaming his team for publishing “fake” growth numbers before the midterms.“It was just revealed that the real numbers on the economy, published before the election, were fake, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the government agency that does these numbers,” the president posted on Truth Social.

“The American economy under the Trump administration is doing far better than the good numbers already released.”

The agency Trump appears to be referring to is the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), which sits within the Commerce Department.

The BEA operates with statistical and methodological independence, a safeguard designed to protect the accuracy and impartiality of its statistics.

On Wednesday, the BEA issued revisions to its growth figures for the third quarter of 2026, saying GDP was 4.3%—not the 3.9% it had originally forecast. The upward revision of 0.9% on the initial estimate was “primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending.”

Analysts are unlikely to be surprised. Revisions are a routine feature of U.S. economic statistics. Lower survey response rates have reduced the precision of some estimates. As UBS’s Pauk Donovan said in a note to clients this morning: “Changes in U.S. economic growth are exaggerated by the fiction of annualization (a technique employed by very few advanced economies).”

“Data revisions are more common as structural change and poor survey response rates reduce precision.”

But President Trump suggested there were more nefarious reasons for the near-percentage-point difference in initial estimates to the published figures: “Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation. This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error.”

Lutnick issued a bullish economic update. Writing on X, the Commerce Secretary said: “We’re bringing American manufacturing back at a scale nobody thought possible. America’s successes will become even more powerful in the coming years as these projects move from groundbreaking to full production.”

Trump’s latest clash with federal data agencies could further undermine confidence in U.S. economic statistics. In 2025, the president fired the director of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Erika McEntarfer, claiming she had overseen the publishing of “phony” job numbers for political reasons. (The president provided no evidence for his claim.)

This, paired with Trump’s extraordinary attacks on the Federal Reserve under former chairman Jerome Powell, led many economists and investors to worry about the credibility of major U.S. institutions that either inform policy or make it.

At the time, Alberto Cavallo, Professor at Harvard Business School, told Goldman Sachs: “It’s difficult to avoid a comparison to the experience of my home country, Argentina, nearly two decades ago when the president, dismayed at rising inflation, removed statistical agency leadership.

“Some statistics stopped being reported, and official data no longer seemed to align with perceptions. That was a very chaotic period that destroyed trust in Argentina’s official statistics for over a decade.”

While Cavallo said the U.S. is ahead of some of Argentina’s data bodies in terms of skills and institutional checks and balances, he said the situation was still “very concerning.”

#5379. In 2026, many employers are ditching merit-based pay bumps in favor of ‘peanut butter raises’

Professionals have long been taught a simple formula for career success: work hard, outperform your peers, and bigger paychecks will follow. But this year, employers are planning to reward their star staffers differently; instead of factoring in merit, more companies are considering general pay hikes spread out evenly, dubbed the “peanut butter raises” trend.

Around 44% of employers plan to roll out uniform, across-the-board wage bumps in 2026, according to a 2026 Payscale report. About 16% of organizations are newly implementing these “peanut butter” raises: 9% say they already employ the pay strategy, and another 18% of organizations are considering it this year. And top-performing companies are all-in on the approach. Around 56% of organizations that reported that they would exceed their revenue goals in 2025 are using or actively considering peanut butter pay increases.

Companies are still planning to boost employee pay by 3.5%, the same rate as last year. And while 48% of businesses will continue the tradition of awarding pay bumps based on worker performance—which the report described as a “best practice”—the new compensation fad may be trying to alleviate financial headwinds for low-paid workers.

“Tying merit pay increases to performance ratings has come under criticism in recent years for being too subjective and prone to bias,” the Payscale report noted. “At the same time, some organizations have made headlines by electing to standardize pay increases to alleviate administrative burden and reward workers equally, especially for low wage workers where inflation is a big concern.”

Job seekers and staffers alike are suffering through a difficult labor market: Hiring has slowed, layoffs are steadily streaming in, and wages don’t feel like they’re holding up. Looking at the year ahead, the picture doesn’t look too pretty.

Wall Street analysts and business executives have been floating the idea we’re in a “K-shaped economy”; higher-income Americans are witnessing their earnings and wealth rise, while lower-income people are struggling against smaller gains and the high cost of living. The concept has come to explain the confusing U.S. economy, where solid overall growth contrasts with sluggish hiring and rising unemployment.

While U.S. companies are holding their average salary increase budget steady at 3.5%, according to a 2025 report from Willis Towers Watson, there’s a large cohort that is planning to scale back. Nearly a third of businesses plan to lower their compensation-increase budgets compared to last year, citing a potential recession, dwindling financial performance, and desire for more control over costs.

Last year, one high-profile employer ditched its merit-based raises in favor of a general, flat pay bump. Starbucks announced it would be giving a standard 2% raise to all salaried North American employees in 2025, diverging from the norm that managers have a say in the raises of their direct reports. It was all a part of CEO Brian Niccol’s bid to reduce costs in a broader company turnaround effort.

But Starbucks is just one notable name in a growing list of employers hunkering down for economic hardship. Lexi Clarke, Payscale’s chief people officer, told Fortune last year that pay-increase budgets are being slimmed as tariffs and economic woes create uncertainty, forcing many employers to be on their guard.

“Economic concerns have now overtaken labor competition as the primary driver of compensation decisions,” Clarke said, as “66% of employers cite this as the reason for pulling back, up 17% from last year.”

As more companies trim back wage budgets and hand out peanut butter raises, there are many still reinvesting in their star talent. America’s largest private employer, $988 billion retail titan Walmart, unrolled a strategy in 2024 to pay its top store managers up to $620,000 per year.

U.S. CEO John Furner said it was a way to “make managers feel like owners,” acknowledging their success with a slice of the profit pie. Their average base pay was hiked from $130,000 to $160,000, raising their total compensation to between $420,000 and $620,000 annually.

And with more than 4,000 store managers across the U.S. (and around 1.5 million workers) when the policy went into effect, the payout wasn’t just generous—it was a calculated bet on culture.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on February 2, 2026.

#5378. Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am

In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals issue ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”

Last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t update for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

There’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

#5377. I have a front-row seat to Norway’s cutting-edge AI newsroom experiment. Even with AI on more than 200 stories a day, a human still checks every one

Christoph Trattner is a professor of information science at the University of Bergen and the founding director of SFI MediaFutures, a research center for responsible media technology. Schibsted Media and Bergens Tidende are partners in the center and help fund it, and he is preparing a funding application with Fjell-Ljom.

Every day, Norway’s largest newspaper, VG, asks an AI model to suggest a headline, search terms and other details for each of its roughly 200 new articles. Before a journalist sees anything, a second model checks the first. In October, across all the newsrooms that use the system, it rejected about one in six of the first model’s attempts. Then the journalist checks the suggestion, and so does an editor, depending on how the newsroom is set up. The cheapest checker goes first, and the people who answer for the story still go last.

“Keep a human in the loop” has become the standard answer to AI’s mistakes. I wanted to know what that human costs, so I asked three Norwegian news organizations what it takes, and whether that has gone up or down as the tools improved. What I learned is that the cost of a check depends heavily on who does it, and on how close that person is to the original work.

I direct a research center on media technology in Norway, where newsrooms began publishing AI-written summaries in 2023. The answers come from the AI Foundations unit at Schibsted Media, the group that owns VG and the regional daily Bergens Tidende; from an editor at Bergens Tidende; and from an editor at Fjell-Ljom, a small local paper in the mountain town of Røros. I am not a neutral observer here: Schibsted Media and Bergens Tidende are partners in my center and help fund it, and I am preparing a grant application with Fjell-Ljom.

Nobody had a measured figure, and the numbers that exist elsewhere come from surveys, not stopwatches. But in one newsroom I could set the check against the work it replaces.

At Bergens Tidende, known as BT, reporters publish 15 to 20 stories of their own a day. AI is not, for now, permitted to write them, but it does write a short version of the finished story, which the reporter is responsible for checking before an editor checks it too. Jan Stian Vold, BT’s development editor, estimates that a reporter who knows the story needs anything from a few seconds to a couple of minutes, and that the editor’s look adds a minute or two. Writing the short version by hand, he told me, takes a reporter three to five minutes. These are his estimates, not measurements. Still, for the person who wrote the story, checking the machine’s version takes less time than writing one.

Vold’s guess is that about one short version in ten needs a fix, and he says the summaries have kept improving with the models. The usual problem is clumsy grammar, or a summary that misses what the reporter considers the most important point. “Almost never hallucinations,” he wrote to me. As far as BT knows, it has never published a critical mistake this way.

Office workers describe something different. In a Workday survey of 3,200 employees who use AI at large companies, nearly 40% of the time AI saved was lost to rework. In a survey of 1,150 U.S. employees by researchers at BetterUp and Stanford, each piece of workslop, AI-generated work that looks finished and is not, took nearly two hours to deal with. These are self-reports about longer documents, not a like-for-like comparison with a newsroom summary. But one difference stands out. In the office, the check often falls to someone who did not do the work and first has to find out what a right answer would look like. At BT, it falls to the one person who already knows.

A Georgia Tech researcher argued this month that catching AI’s mistakes is a mental burden that eats the gains. In the one newsroom where I could estimate it, the check took less time than the writing it replaced, and the reason is who does the checking.

Johanna Johansson, who works in AI Foundations at Schibsted Media, told me that “hallucinations are surprisingly common.” Vold had written “almost never.” Both can be right. She was speaking of AI-generated content in general, he of one narrow task, the summary of a text the reporter has just finished. Two things may be at work here, and I cannot separate them: a narrow task may produce fewer errors, and a checker who knows the material may spot the ones that remain faster.

On one point they agree. “Generally we always have a human in the loop,” Johansson said. That was always a firm principle, she said, and the huge improvements in the models have not made it any less important.

A judgment call, I would add, is the kind of error that only someone who knows the story is likely to notice.

So has the checking gone up or down? For BT’s newsroom as a whole, Vold could not say. His own work is administration and presentations, not journalism, and there his checking has gone down as he has learned to use AI as an assistant and not as a source of facts. At Fjell-Ljom it has stayed constant, because it was never a separate step. What nobody described is letting go of the check on what gets published.

I think they are right to hold that line, and the reason goes beyond the errors that remain. The check at BT is cheap because of everything the reporter did before the summary appeared. Hand the same summary to someone who had not reported the story, and the check would either take far longer or turn into a formality. A freelance journalist interviewed for a 2025 master’s thesis at Aalto University made a similar point: typing out an interview word for word “really gets you inside it in a way that reading over a transcription and just checking for errors doesn’t.”

For companies outside the news business, I take three things from this. Count the check: how many items, how many people look at each one, and how many minutes each look takes. Then set that against what the task took before. Do not treat a falling error rate as permission to stop checking. Nobody I asked has. Above all, give the check to the person who knows the work, instead of adding a reviewer downstream who has to start from nothing. In these newsrooms, that is what keeps the check manageable.

As AI takes over more of what comes before the check, I would worry less about the minutes than about whether anyone is left who can tell in seconds that something is wrong.

#5374. Hurt By Inflation? Here Are 13 Real-World Ways To Cut Costs In Your Business

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

With inflation still running hot, these simple moves can trim your business costs without slowing you down.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Inflation remains stubborn. Producer prices are now running at a 6.5% annual clip, and affordability is top of mind. Want to cut some costs in your business? Of course you do.  Try these moves.

Both ChatGPT and Claude offer connections to your bank account and credit card services. Or, if you’re nervous about that, just upload your statements.  You’ll be impressed by the number of suggestions they make to reduce your spending and better manage expenses.

I used to think canceling online subscriptions would be a big headache, and years ago it was. Not anymore. Search for “cancel my subscription on Google Play” (or Apple or Amazon), and you’ll get direct links to do it. I’m betting you and your business have subscriptions you’ve forgotten about that are eating up hundreds of dollars a year.

Every year, put your business and auto insurance policies out for a quote. Ask your AI chatbot to make suggestions too. This is not very time-consuming and can be accomplished using an administrative person in your office. We’re oftentimes too lazy to do this.  And that’s costing us.

Many of my clients have complicated, expensive coffee machines in their break rooms with a wide variety of coffees. They also stock sugar packets, teas, mini creamers, plastic stirrers and paper cups. It’s too much. Offer fewer coffees so you order less. Put out a sugar bowl, bring in a gallon of creamer and go back to ceramic mugs. Call me Scrooge, but it saves money.

NerdWallet does a great job regularly reviewing business and personal credit cards. Again, use your AI chatbot to look at your spending and tell it your preferences and you’ll get plenty of recommendations too.  Moving to a better card could earn you more points and cashback rewards then you’re getting right now. I have some clients that regularly switch back and forth.

Speaking of credit, if your business buys products on Amazon, then make sure you use one of Amazon’s credit cards for purchases.  With a Prime membership, you can earn 5% back on eligible Amazon purchases, and there’s no annual fee.

If you can’t pay off a credit card purchase right away from operations, consider using working capital or a lower-rate loan to reduce the balance. Credit card interest rates are high, so this can cut what you pay in interest significantly.

This is a very common tax move, yet so many of us ignore it. Put as much as you can into your retirement plan to lower your tax bill this year.  When you save – assuming you’re eligible – sock money into a Roth IRA or Roth 401K so your after-tax money grows tax-free.  With a Roth, there are no minimum distributions, and you can take the money out whenever you want, provided it meets certain requirements like a first-time home purchase, higher education or unreimbursed medical expenses.

Make sure your company has an HSA and contribute the max. It will reduce your tax expense and allow you to save money for future healthcare expenses.

Every square foot your inventory takes up costs you in overhead and space. Twice a year, take a hard look at your inventory and get rid of what isn’t moving. Sell it on Craigslist, eBay or Facebook Marketplace or scrap it.

Mark Cuban’s Cost Plus Drugs and Amazon Pharmacy both offer options that let businesses provide discounted prescription drugs, and they work with many popular health plans.

Set up a donor-advised fund and contribute to it this year, even if you haven’t decided which charities or nonprofits will receive the money. You take the deduction now and choose the recipients later.

I like Capital One Shopping. Add it as a browser extension for yourself and anyone else who makes purchases for your business. Whenever someone is on a shopping site, it searches for available coupons before you buy. It works about half the time, and it has saved me significant money over the years.

We can all afford the things we want — it’s just that sometimes we choose to spend our money on other things instead. That’s fine. But know that cutting back on things like travel, entertainment, subscriptions, marketing or other discretionary spending in your business (and your personal life) can help you reallocate your cash for other purposes.  You’re more in control than you think.

Inflation remains stubborn. Producer prices are now running at a 6.5% annual clip, and affordability is top of mind. Want to cut some costs in your business? Of course you do.  Try these moves.

Both ChatGPT and Claude offer connections to your bank account and credit card services. Or, if you’re nervous about that, just upload your statements.  You’ll be impressed by the number of suggestions they make to reduce your spending and better manage expenses.

I used to think canceling online subscriptions would be a big headache, and years ago it was. Not anymore. Search for “cancel my subscription on Google Play” (or Apple or Amazon), and you’ll get direct links to do it. I’m betting you and your business have subscriptions you’ve forgotten about that are eating up hundreds of dollars a year.

#5373. Chanel’s CEO Leena Nair makes the case for human made ‘beauty and creation.’ In an era of AI saturation, her $19 billion-a-year business depends on it

The chief executive of one of the world’s leading fashion brands has said that the intense and often slow process of craftswomen and men making products by hand has become a vital skill in a world of online “instant gratification.”

Leena Nair, the CEO of Chanel, said that business leaders are living through an “unprecedented” period of transformation and fragility, adding that it was time to prioritize human ingenuity and talent.

“Macro-economic shifts, huge leaps in AI and technology and geopolitical instability, these are challenges affecting all sectors,” she told the annual gala dinner of the French Chamber of Great Britain, which brings together U.K. and French business executives, policy makers, and cultural leaders.

“And in this context of disruption, the power of creation and beauty has never been more vital or more precious. Creation and beauty have been vital sources of inspiration and joy for thousands of years. They’re even more precious today in a world of constant instant gratification, constant overstimulation, and infinite touch points.”

Nair, who has been Chanel CEO since 2022, saw the luxury brand return to growth last year, led by an increase in sales in America. Global revenues rose by 1.8% compared with 2024 to $19.3 billion, while operating profits rose 5.2% to $4.7 billion.

Nair said there was a growing body of scientific evidence that revealed that exposure to art and human-led creative work led to higher levels of happiness and performance.

“This growing body of academic research shows how encounters with beauty correlate directly to a greater sense of human flourishing at work and in life,” she said. “In recent years, we see growing scientific evidence of the improving impact that arts and culture has on physical and mental well-being.”

“In this context of disruption, the power of creation and beauty has never been more vital or more precious”

Over 95% of Chanel’s customers are women, Nair said, adding that “beauty” is a very important driver of how people respond to the world around them. She said that one customer who had been through surgery said that buying crafted products was part of her recovery.

“Surgeons tell me this all the time, that when surgery is over they know the women are back to normal when they ask to put on their makeup for the first time,” she said.

Many leaders of luxury brands often feel ignored when it comes to policy debates about economic growth. In the U.K., the end of foreign visitors being able to shop without incurring the national sales tax has caused controversy. In the U.S., new tariffs targeting luxury goods have unsettled markets.

“Luxury is an economic powerhouse, it’s a cultural powerhouse and an emotional powerhouse,” Nair said. “To put that scale into context, European high-end luxury brands generate a trillion dollars in business every year. That’s 5% of Europe’s GDP. “It’s not a niche sector. More than 2 million people work in the sector across Europe.”

Chanel works with the King’s Foundation, King Charles III’s organization that supports the retention and development of traditional skills.

“It looks simple, but to do a pleated skirt takes eight hours of pushing a cardboard mold back and forth by two talented artisans doing it the right way,” Nair said, arguing that Chanel continues to invest in “skills that will otherwise be lost, working with extraordinary artisans and partners, many of whom we have worked with for generations.”

Kamal Ahmed is the executive editorial director of Europe and the Middle East. Kamal is the author of Letter from London, Fortune Europe's weekly take on global business as seen from London. Previously, he was director of audio at The Telegraph and presenter of The Daily T podcast.

#5372. Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

The new funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

“The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis said the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight company acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis said.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The company isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders said. A second, larger site using AMD’s new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The company says it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan said that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a new AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he said.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

The $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis said the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one big customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”

Updated at 6:20 a.m. PT with Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.

#5371. 5 trends that will define 2027—and how to invest in them

The AI buildout and the weight-loss drug boom are still going strong. But higher interest rates, uncertainty over defense spending, and a rush to build solar projects could reward investors in less obvious places.

Heraclitus, the Greek philosopher, is often credited with the idea that the only constant in life is change. He was writing around 500 BC, but he could just as easily have been describing 2027, a year poised to bring seismic shifts in politics, technology, markets, and the way we live and work. Some of what’s coming is already in plain sight, like the AI revolution. Other forces are quieter but could prove just as consequential, including a likely surge in solar construction. Here are the five trends Fortune believes will define the coming year, and how investors can position themselves for each.

In 2024, it appeared that pandemic-era inflation had been tamed, and the Federal Reserve responded with a series of cuts to its benchmark interest rate. This optimism didn’t last, however, and price shocks from tariffs and the Iran war led the Fed to boost rates in 2026. The central bank is expected to continue on this path.

This is glum news for homebuyers and the real estate industry, and for sectors including AI, which count on cheap credit to keep their businesses humming. But high interest rates are not bad for everyone. Beneficiaries include individual savers, who can look forward to higher income, and big banks whose business involves lending money.

While banks tend to earn more from loans when rates are higher, it is the “goliath” banks that do best in these environments, said Mike Mayo, head of U.S. large-cap bank research at Wells Fargo Securities. For 2027, Mayo said JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and Bank of America (BAC), in particular, appear poised for a strong year based on bullish guidance they have issued. But he cautions that high interest rates only act as a tailwind up to a point—and that a rapid series of hikes would put larger portions of the economy under strain, counteracting the positive effect of higher interest rates for banks.

Mayo dismissed concerns over new technologies, such as yield-seeking AI agents that could threaten the deposit base of the biggest banks such as Citigroup (C) and Wells Fargo (WFC). “The death of large banks has been exaggerated for 50 years,” he said. “Their deposit franchises have become bigger over time, and the reason is trust. Trust is more important than Big Tech.”

This trust in established financial institutions, along with big banks’ aversion to risk in general, are likely to serve the banks especially well at a time of mounting unease over cybersecurity—the result of a spate of recent incidents, including ones involving rogue AI agents. In this context, the “goliath” banks may draw investors looking for a safe and steady play.

And while their performance trailed the broader S&P 500 in 2026, the Big Four banks delivered on another attribute that investors value: large and reliable dividends.

It’s been about four years since OpenAI’s launch of ChatGPT set off a massive rally in AI stocks. Some investors are getting jitters about the scope of the AI build-out amid fears that it’s a bubble—especially after the blue wave midterms elected a slew of Democrats on promises to rein in the AI industry. Still, the tech behemoths at the center of the boom—including Meta Platforms, Microsoft, and Amazon—are going full speed.

In this environment, looking for opportunities is not about deciding whether artificial intelligence is the future (spoiler alert: It is). The real question is which companies are positioned to succeed, no matter the pace of the AI build-out.

In this context, Bernstein senior analyst Stacy Rasgon likes the chipmaker Broadcom (AVGO) because its stock is “very, very cheap,” he told Fortune. The stock, like that of other chipmakers, sold off sharply in late 2026 as investors questioned how long the AI spending frenzy can last, even though earnings expectations remain strong.

Fellow chipmaker Nvidia’s shares took a major hit in November following revelations that its CEO, Jensen Huang, had acknowledged an affair, while the company opened an investigation into reports that he had been targeted by Chinese intelligence. Huang resigned from the company he cofounded four days later.

Applied Materials (AMAT) is another stock that may offer considerable upside. The company sells equipment to manufacture chips, positioning Applied Materials to benefit from infrastructure investments in advanced processors, memory, and chip packaging. “It’s very clear to me that we need a lot more equipment,” said Rasgon.

That doesn’t mean these companies won’t face potential headwinds in 2027. Arun Sundaram, an investment strategist at CFRA, points to potential energy bottlenecks and concerns that higher interest rates could make AI financing more expensive. He cites political pushback against data center construction as another potential obstacle—opposition that will only increase as Democrats, many of whom have been vocal critics of the AI industry, take power in Congress.

Still, analysts like Rasgon remain optimistic. He pointed to third-quarter earnings from Big Tech, which included more AI spending and a surge in cloud revenues. “As it turns out, a lot of these companies may be more profitable than people thought. They’re actually generating money,” he said. “From a fundamental level, we’ll probably see sustainability in spending … Whether or not sentiment from a stock standpoint is going to buy into that or not, I don’t know yet. But that’s going to be the key debate.”

Most of our recommendations point you toward stocks or sectors to buy. When it comes to the defense industry in 2027 you might be well served to do the opposite: Stay on the sidelines. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine dragged into its fifth year in February 2026. That same month, the U.S. and Israel launched a war against Iran, triggering retaliatory attacks across the Middle East. By early summer, there was anxious talk in Washington, D.C., about depleted stocks of missiles and other munitions.

In such an environment, investors might expect the shares of large defense companies to be soaring. That’s not the case. Even as demand for weapons has grown and a slew of techy startups have entered the sector, the stock prices of the big military contractors known as the “primes”—including RTX, Northrop Grumman, and General Dynamics—have largely flailed. Only one of these companies, Lockheed Martin, outperformed the S&P. Shares of Boeing, which has a sizable division that sells to the military, lagged the index by 30%.

High interest rates are glum news for homebuyers and the real estate and AI industries, but individual savers and big banks can benefit—up to a point

The reason for this lackluster performance is ongoing uncertainty over U.S. defense spending, said Peter Arment, a senior analyst at Baird. While the Pentagon and President Donald Trump are keen to pass a massive allocation for the military, it’s unclear where the money to pay for it would come from. Meanwhile, many in the incoming freshman class of Democrats vocally oppose Trump’s military policies.

While there is a tradition of bipartisan support for the military in Congress, this may not translate into a major defense bill in 2027, Arment said. Instead, lawmakers may rely on ad hoc measures that don’t include significant military spending.

We’ve all heard the buzz about GLP-1s, the blockbuster category of drugs that are delivering dramatic results in treating obesity and Type 2 diabetes. In 2027, the medications—sold under brand names including Ozempic and Wegovy—are poised to reach even more patients as insurance coverage expands and pills offer an alternative to injections.

JPMorgan forecasts that the global market for incretin-based drugs, which include GLP-1s, will reach $200 billion by 2030. In the U.S., the bank predicts that the number of patients taking these drugs will jump from roughly 10 million in 2025 to 25 million by the end of the decade.

This rise will be driven in part by expanded Medicare access. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, which launched in July and runs through December 2027, offers certain weight-management drugs for $50 a month.

GLP-1 in pill form could draw more users, too. Novo Nordisk’s oral Wegovy won FDA approval in December 2025, followed by Eli Lilly’s Foundayo in April 2026. Both are taken daily and could appeal to people who have held off on the treatment because they don’t like injections.

Lilly (LLY) and Novo (NVO) stocks stand to benefit the most. Both sell injectable and oral weight-loss treatments, and have spent years building the manufacturing facilities needed to meet demand. Lilly has committed more than $50 billion to U.S. manufacturing since 2020. It would take years for smaller would-be rivals to reach this scale. That business “moat” should help Lilly and Novo hold on to their lead, Evan Seigerman, BMO’s head of health care research, told Fortune: “I think that those two are poised to really maintain the lion’s share of the market in 2027,” he said. “You don’t see anyone else coming to take that share.”

For investors looking for a picks-and-shovels play outside of the drugmakers themselves, West Pharmaceutical Services (WST) is an option. The company sells injectable-drug components like stoppers, plungers, and seals. Wall Street has taken notice: In November, Jefferies called the stock a buy and hiked its price target.

Those who assumed the solar sector was dead are missing out on one of the more surprising twists of 2027. Amid ongoing tensions in the Middle East, demand for energy is stronger than ever, and that is good news for solar power.

Solar companies are also poised to benefit from developers rushing to meet a key end-of-2027 deadline for federal clean-electricity tax credits. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 established the clean-electricity tax credits, but President Donald Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act accelerated their expiration. Projects that began construction after July 4, 2026, must be placed in service by the end of 2027; those that began construction on or before that date can qualify even if they come online later, subject to other requirements. The investment credit generally covers 30% of qualifying costs for projects, with additional bonuses available. Developers can alternatively claim a credit based on electricity production.

A rush by solar installers to meet the end-of-2027 deadline is likely to boost sales for First Solar (FSLR), which makes electricity-generating panels, and for Nextpower (NXT) and Array Technologies (ARRY), which sell tracking systems that help panels follow the sun.

Regardless of how many installers meet the solar tax credit deadline, overall energy consumption will rise in 2027. UBS projects this will lead to 310 gigawatts of combined U.S. solar and wind additions through 2030, driven partly by power-hungry data centers and industrial customers. Goldman Sachs forecasts global data center power demand will rise 220% from 2023 levels by 2030.

Natural gas could help meet that demand, but there has been a surge in orders for the gas turbines that power data centers, meaning delivery can take years. Case in point: GE Vernova, a leading maker of this heavy-duty machinery, was already taking orders for 2031 in July 2026.

Those long lead times could give solar an opening. Gregory Nemet, a professor at the University of Wisconsin, told Fortune that developers planning data centers in the next few years may choose solar if they cannot get these turbines. “That dynamic is pretty consequential to how fast solar grows,” Nemet said.

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of Fortune.

Morgan Chittum is a reporter at Fortune covering finance.

Jeff John Roberts is the Finance and Crypto editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of the blockchain and how technology is changing finance.

#5370. Most Unicorns Are Worth More Than Their Last Funding-Round Valuations, Crunchbase Estimates

The more than 1,900 startups on the The Crunchbase Unicorn Board have a combined valuation of roughly $9 trillion, based on their last reported valuations. But Crunchbase’s new Current Valuation Model, which estimates how private-company values have changed since their last funding rounds, puts that figure closer to $11 trillion.

Most unicorns are estimated to have gained value, even as others have lost ground, our analysis shows. Among the biggest potential gainers are AI startups Thinking Machines Lab, whose estimated value has climbed from $12 billion to $40 billion, and Sierra, from nearly $16 billion to $31.5 billion.

The majority of companies on the board are valued higher by the Current Valuations model than they were when they last raised funding. Only around 236 companies — roughly 12% of the board — are down by more than $100 million in value compared to their last reported valuations.

The valuation model estimates that a select group of 24 companies have gained more than $10 billion in value since their most recent funding rounds. They include Mira Murati’s AI research lab Thinking Machines Lab, which was last valued at $12 billion in its 2025 seed funding but has a current valuation projected at $40 billion.

Similarly, Bret Taylor’s customer oriented AI agent builder Sierra was last valued at close to $16  billion in a May 2026 funding round. It is now estimated to be valued at $31.5 billion, per the Crunchbase model. (On Monday, Bloomberg reported that Sierra is raising a new round at a roughly $30 billion valuation.)

Physical Intelligence, a company building AI for robotics, was valued at $5.6 billion in its Series B. Crunchbase’s Current Valuation model estimates its valuation now at $18.5 billion.

Another 53 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $5 billion to just under $10 billion higher than those achieved in their most recent funding rounds. They include Unconventional AI, which is focused on energy efficiency for AI; Lila Sciences, which is building artificial intelligence for science; AI cloud company Vultr; AI research lab humans&; stablecoin payment platform Tempo; and Yann LeCun’s Advanced Machine Intelligence, which is modeling physical world intelligence.

A total of 484 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $1 billion to $5 billion higher than their most recent funding valuations. More than 1,100 companies have values that were flat or up to $1 billion higher than their most recent funding valuations.

Only around 236 companies are estimated to be below their most recent valuation, by more than $100 million. Collectively, their current valuations are down by $326 billion from their most recent fundings, Crunchbase estimates.

The Crunchbase Unicorn Board reached its highest value in 2026 as three companies approached or exceeded $1 trillion valuations — unprecedented in the board’s history. The board peaked at $10 trillion in advance of the Anthropic IPO this past week. The company’s public-market debut removed close to $1 trillion from the board. This followed another trillion-dollar exit from the board earlier this year, when SpaceX — last valued at $1.3 trillion in a secondary financing this year — before it went public in June at a value of $1.8 trillion.

All told, the unicorn board this year is currently up by $1.5 trillion from its $7.5 trillion value at the end of 2025. With its closest rival now on the public markets, OpenAI is currently the most highly valued private company at an official valuation of $1.25 trillion.

The unicorn board has picked up pace this year. Around 360 companies joined the board so far this year, the second highest count in a single year after 2021 when 621 companies joined.

A faster pace of new entrants and rising valuations have helped replenish the board, while current estimates suggest substantial additional value has accumulated between funding rounds.

The next test is how closely these estimated values align with prices investors are willing to pay. Future funding rounds, secondary transactions, public listings and M&A will reveal how much of the board’s estimated $2 trillion uplift translates into realized value.

Current valuations are based on the new Crunchbase Current Valuation Model, which prices companies using a proprietary machine learning model that starts with a company’s most recent post-money valuation and continuously estimates how its value has shifted since that funding event. The model covers roughly 230,000 funded private companies. Read more here.

#5369. Microsoft’s Brad Smith on Trump’s data center tax threat: ‘You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith said the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he said most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which says it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

His reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu

He gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

His one example was an unnamed company that wants to build in Finland. Google announced a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, said he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a big technology transfer offshore.”

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the company for a briefing.

Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate company, and said Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Smith said Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

He put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered important.

Outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He said the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he said much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.)

Smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.
