#5353. How To Build Influence Without Waiting for Authority

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Building influence requires more than a leadership title or strong job performance. By developing relationships, gathering evidence, earning trust and taking initiative, professionals can shape decisions, create meaningful change and establish themselves as leaders before receiving formal authority.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Early in my career, I believed excellent work would eventually create its own reward. I became the person people trusted to solve problems, take on difficult assignments and deliver when the stakes were high. Yet there is a trap hidden inside reliability: You can become indispensable to the work without becoming influential in the decisions that determine it.

I eventually learned to separate authority from influence. Authority comes with a title or responsibility for the final decision. Influence is your ability to move an idea, change an outcome or bring people with you regardless of what appears beneath your name in an email signature.

That distinction matters because waiting for authority can consume years. Influence can begin from almost any position, including one far from the executive table.

When I enter an organization as a consultant, I spend the early stretch watching. I want to understand who people consult before making a decision, whose objections carry weight and who has direct access to the person making the final call.

The organizational chart provides useful information, but it rarely shows the full picture. I think of the real structure as a web. To start mapping yours, study a few decisions and ask:

Write down what you observe. Look for patterns rather than focusing only on seniority. This helps you see where your relationships and contributions can have greater impact and where you may have been spending energy with little effect on the final outcome.

I learned this while working to improve outcomes for Black women inside an organization. During my first several months, I created programs, workshops and employee groups. Leadership was pleased, yet I could see that we were addressing individual women while leaving larger cultural problems untouched.

Instead of walking into an executive meeting and declaring that the approach needed to change, I gathered evidence. I examined exit interviews, studied promotion patterns, found allies prepared for deeper change and ran small pilots that demonstrated another approach.

By the time I pushed for a larger change, I had evidence, results and people behind me. Over roughly 18 months, the work became more strategic because I had built the influence required to change how the problem was understood.

Before making your next significant proposal, gather three things:

An idea becomes harder to dismiss when other people can see what you see. Building support early also gives people an opportunity to improve the idea before you bring it into a higher-stakes conversation.

Being excellent at your job creates credibility, but credibility alone can leave you with more assignments rather than greater impact. People know you will deliver, so they keep handing you things to deliver. Eventually, being the dependable person can become its own holding pattern.

Use the trust you have earned to shape the work itself. Propose an improvement, ask to participate earlier in a project or volunteer to lead an initiative that connects you with people outside your immediate team. Keep a record of problems solved, measurable outcomes and moments when colleagues sought your judgment.

Credibility sitting still makes you useful. Credibility applied to decisions expands your influence.

Many professionals concentrate their relationship-building efforts on senior executives. Yet influence rarely travels through a single relationship. Peers, colleagues in other departments, administrative professionals and people closer to customers can all help an idea move.

The Revolutionary Pathmakers I write about have historically created networks through community and cross-functional relationships when conventional pathways were unavailable. Those relationships provided information, support and opportunities that formal structures alone failed to provide.

This is not just history. My research found that Black women who lead from values rather than position build more sustainable authority than traditional power-based models, with higher retention and better long-term results. When the formal channels are closed, influence built through relationships and shared values is not the backup plan. It turns out to be the stronger one.

Identify two people outside your usual circle and learn what they are trying to accomplish. Ask what repeatedly creates difficulty for them and where your work intersects. Enter those conversations looking for ways to contribute rather than immediately asking for something.

Influence grows when people experience your contribution before you need their support.

I often coach people who describe having little power while simultaneously outlining solutions they can put into motion. The question I ask is simple: What can you responsibly begin from where you are?

You might test one part of an idea, improve a recurring process, connect people working separately or gather evidence around a problem nobody owns. Start small enough that the idea can prove itself, then document the result. Pay attention to what worked, who benefited and what would be required to expand it.

A successful experiment gives you something stronger than a proposal about what might work. It gives you evidence of what already did.

I spent years being excellent while being overlooked. What changed my trajectory was understanding that waiting for recognition was delaying the leadership I was already capable of practicing.

Influence grows when you understand how decisions move, build relationships before you need them, use your credibility intentionally and create opportunities to demonstrate what you can do. These actions can begin well before a promotion appears.

There is one more piece, and it may be the one that matters most. Moral clarity. The influence that lasts belongs to people who stand for something bigger than their own advancement. When you are clear about what you are for, and consistent about it, people follow you because of what you represent, not just what you can do for them. Authority can be granted. Moral authority has to be earned, and it is the kind no one can take back.

A title can expand your authority, but your ability to make an impact can begin long before anyone changes the words beneath your name. The question is whether you will wait for that change or start using the influence you already have.

Early in my career, I believed excellent work would eventually create its own reward. I became the person people trusted to solve problems, take on difficult assignments and deliver when the stakes were high. Yet there is a trap hidden inside reliability: You can become indispensable to the work without becoming influential in the decisions that determine it.

I eventually learned to separate authority from influence. Authority comes with a title or responsibility for the final decision. Influence is your ability to move an idea, change an outcome or bring people with you regardless of what appears beneath your name in an email signature.

That distinction matters because waiting for authority can consume years. Influence can begin from almost any position, including one far from the executive table.

#5352. SenseNet lands $43M financing deal for early wildfire detection and intelligence

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:47 am

SenseNet, a startup providing wildfire detection and intelligence, on Tuesday announced a $43 million financing package. The Vancouver, B.C.-based company says the funding will support its expansion across the U.S. and internationally.

The startup uses a suite of technologies for the rapid detection of wildfires, including environmental sensors, AI-enabled cameras, satellite data, drone technology and predictive analytics. Its monitoring footprint covers 450 million acres in a dozen countries.

SenseNet says its technology has provided early alerts for more than 10,000 fires, in some cases hours before the first 911 calls.

“Wildfire protection is no longer just about detecting a fire as quickly as possible. It’s about understanding what’s happening, what could happen next, and giving the right people the information they need to act,” Hamed Noori, co-founder and CEO of SenseNet, said in a statement.

Noori launched SenseNet in 2019 with Chief Technology Officer Shahab Bahrami. Both hold doctorates in electrical and computer engineering from the University of British Columbia.

The Series B round was led by Idealist Capital, with participation from Fusion Fund, Stormbreaker Ventures, Thin Line Capital, National Bank of Canada and The Sitka Foundation.

The financing includes purchases of newly issued shares, which put money into SenseNet; secondary share sales, which pay existing shareholders; and debt. SenseNet did not disclose how much of the $43 million falls into each category.

The startup previously raised $12.78 million and has 30 employees, according to PitchBook.

SenseNet competes with companies including OroraTech, Dryad and Pano AI, whose cameras, software and alerting services are used by Washington’s Department of Natural Resources to detect wildfires. The companies are developing their technology as warming temperatures and drier conditions increase wildfire risks.

#5351. Your Career Is Probably Ignoring Your Strongest Leadership Training: Community

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Community involvement can be a powerful source of leadership skills, professional connections and career opportunities. By recognizing the value of their community experiences, building genuine relationships and making clear requests for support, professionals can turn existing connections into lasting career growth and influence.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For years, one of the communities shaping my leadership was one I barely counted as professional development: my church. I coordinated programs, worked with volunteers, managed limited resources and built agreement among people with different opinions. Somehow, I still placed those experiences in a separate category from my career.

That separation caused me to overlook something valuable. The places where we live, worship, volunteer, parent and serve can develop serious leadership capabilities while connecting us with people who know how we show up over time. My research has found that Black women with active community relationships can gain professional opportunities through those relationships while developing skills that translate directly into their careers.

The opportunity is bigger than having a large contact list. Professional power grows when you recognize the value already present in your community and learn how to carry it into other parts of your life.

Church taught me things about leadership that no corporate workshop could replicate. Try coordinating people who volunteer their time, have strong opinions and can leave whenever they want. You quickly learn how to communicate, build agreement and keep people moving when a title gives you very little leverage.

I see similar experiences when I work with clients. A mother may sit on several school committees. Someone else coaches youth sports, organizes neighborhood events or leads a sorority chapter. Because these responsibilities happen outside an employer, people frequently discount them.

I offer a simple exercise for changing that perspective. Draw two columns on a piece of paper. On the left, write every meaningful community role you have held. On the right, translate what each role actually required.

The work stays exactly the same. What changes is your ability to recognize and describe its professional value.

My research surfaced another finding that deserves attention. Women carrying significant family and community responsibilities often received professional leads and opportunities through those relationships. Someone they knew from a community group, board, school or family connection thought of them when an opportunity emerged.

This matters because some of the best opportunities begin through conversation before they reach a public job posting. When people have spent time with you in a community setting, they may already know how you handle responsibility, communicate through disagreement or follow through on commitments.

Take inventory of the communities you already participate in and ask:

The goal is greater than finding someone who can get you a job. It is allowing people who already know your character and capabilities to understand the fuller range of what you can contribute.

A quick word on friend raising, which is my name for building genuine, reciprocal relationships instead of collecting contacts. I have written about it at length elsewhere, so I will not repeat it here, except to make one point that matters for conversion. The relationship is the raw material. It is not the finished product.

Someone who has watched you contribute for five years knows something about you that a person who exchanged business cards with you five minutes ago never will. That depth is what makes the translation believable when you finally claim it. But building the relationship and converting it into professional power are two different moves, and most people stop after the first.

Strong relationships can create opportunity, but people still need to know what you need. I see professionals build wonderful communities and then struggle to make the second move. They hope someone will somehow infer that they are exploring a board position, looking for clients or considering a career change.

Be direct. You might tell someone, “I’m interested in serving on a nonprofit board where my experience in organizational change would be useful. If you hear of an organization looking for that background, I’d appreciate you keeping me in mind.”

Then give the other person a graceful way to decline. They may lack the right connection, have limited influence in their organization or simply be unable to help at that moment. A healthy relationship should remain whole regardless of the answer.

Community becomes powerful because relationships exist beyond a single exchange. That means your behavior after an ask matters as much as your behavior before it.

If the first time someone hears from you in years is when you need a favor, you are drawing on a relationship you stopped maintaining. Instead, make reciprocity a regular practice. Check in without an agenda. Celebrate other people’s accomplishments. Offer help when you have something useful to contribute, and continue showing up after someone has helped you.

I once thought my church leadership belonged in one box and my professional leadership belonged in another. Today, I see how artificial that separation was. The skills I practiced in the community were part of the same leadership I carried into organizations, consulting engagements and other areas of my life.

Your community may be a church, school, neighborhood group, cultural organization, alumni association or circle of parents you see every week. Look again at the people and experiences you have been treating as separate from your career. You may discover that some of your strongest professional assets have been developing there for years.

Knowing many people gives you contacts. Building reciprocal relationships, recognizing the leadership they develop and learning how to connect those relationships across your life gives you something far more durable: a community that grows stronger as its members create opportunities for one another.

For years, one of the communities shaping my leadership was one I barely counted as professional development: my church. I coordinated programs, worked with volunteers, managed limited resources and built agreement among people with different opinions. Somehow, I still placed those experiences in a separate category from my career.

That separation caused me to overlook something valuable. The places where we live, worship, volunteer, parent and serve can develop serious leadership capabilities while connecting us with people who know how we show up over time. My research has found that Black women with active community relationships can gain professional opportunities through those relationships while developing skills that translate directly into their careers.

The opportunity is bigger than having a large contact list. Professional power grows when you recognize the value already present in your community and learn how to carry it into other parts of your life.

#5350. Uncommon Thinkers: Saf Rabah wants to make it easier to build housing, one permit at a time

by Grace Kaste on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:50 amNovember 24, 2026 at 1:22 pm

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

When startup founder Safouen (Saf) Rabah decided to get in on the AI boom, he didn’t start by coding or by training any models. He got in touch with urban planners at Bellevue City Hall, and together they combed through nearly 300 land use permit applications to find common mistakes and bottlenecks.

Bellevue began using Rabah’s platform, Govstream.AI, in the summer of 2025, starting with an AI assistant for city staff. In a test using past applications, about three times as many were judged complete with Govstream’s tool. Rabah says that change alone has the potential to alter the housing stock of the city.

“Why can’t we build more housing? All the macro economic reasons, inflation, material costs, labor, land scarcity, are all exacerbated by the slow permitting process,” Rabah said. “That’s what we want to change.”

So, how did Rabah, a B2B software engineer by training, find his way to land use permitting?

Rabah hadn’t heard of the government technology sector, aka GovTech, until mid-career, but looking back, the signs were all there. He was born in Sfax, Tunisia, and grew up in Tunis. Throughout his childhood, he dreamed of running for office.

“I come from a small developing country, so there’s always this idea of, what could a small developing country become? How can it prosper and grow?” Rabah said. “Building has always been a big part of what I imagined myself doing.”

As a teenager in the 1980s, he attended a USAID-funded boarding school in Tunis. The school was part of Cold War efforts to expand American soft power around the Middle East; classes were conducted in English and many of the students went on to university in North America.

“The school had the first Macintosh lab in all of Africa,” Rabah said. “I can still picture the USAID logo on the back of each computer.”

Rabah got a scholarship to University of British Columbia, where he studied electrical engineering while running what he calls his “first entrepreneurial venture”: a service that built and hosted websites for small businesses.

That led to a job at a startup called Pivotal, a customer relationship management platform where Rabah led a team responsible for e-business applications. After Pivotal went public, Rabah left for a job at TELUS, one of Canada’s “big three” telecommunications corporations, but quickly felt frustrated by the dynamics at such a large company.

“Even though I worked on nascent products, it was very, very bureaucratic,” Rabah said. “There were committees, a hundred thousand employees. I missed building things.”

Rabah began to look for a new job that would not only allow him to build but also to make a difference.

“Being an immigrant, it’s always tempting to stay content with having a good job, good status,” Rabah said. “But I’ve always enjoyed the ‘what if?’ mindset, the clean slate. It’s this way today, but could we imagine it to be something different?”

That vision led him to Socrata, which in 2010 was just a nascent government technology startup.

“I really connected with the founder,” Rabah said. “It had a really cool mission, it combined the ‘do-well’ with ‘do-good.’”

Socrata was one of the first platforms to host data portals for local governments and federal agencies, allowing citizens to access and map public data sets. Many U.S. cities, including Seattle, still use Socrata’s software today to publish information including crime logs, permits, and budgets.

“We were a big part of pioneering the open data movement,” Rabah said. “At one point almost every major city was our customer, and half the states.”

Socrata was acquired by Tyler Technologies in 2018, and Rabah stayed on until 2024.

“The funny part is today we use that data quite a lot in our work because one of the most popular data sets that any city publishes is its permit data,” Rabah said. “We’ve even built a connector between Socrata and Govstream.”

But once Socrata was acquired, Rabah began to feel the same way he had at TELUS: boxed in by bureaucracy.

“Tyler was a really good company, but it is a big company,” Rabah said. “Tech was getting repetitive, and I was thinking about leaving it altogether.”

“The thing that pushed me over the edge is that AI happened,” Rabah said. “It was one of those moments where once you start working with it, you really can’t help but think, ‘I can revisit virtually every assumption I’ve made over the last 20 years, every constraint.’”

Immediately, he thought of his passion for building—building a startup, building a better country, and literally building a building.

“I’ve been fascinated by the built environment since my Lego days: What makes some cities livable and others not?” Rabah said. “Then, living in Seattle, you see the lack of housing, affordability, and the homelessness problem we have, and you’re like, why can’t we build more housing? I started believing that these problems are in fact solvable if we simply speed things up and simplify things with AI.”

In July of 2024, Rabah began working with his “design partner,” Bellevue’s Development Services Department, to learn more about common permitting problems.

“We started with something visionary and high-level, but you can only get there if you understand the granular problems of the day-to-day,” Rabah said. “So we talked with developers and builders and we talked with the people on the other side of the counter who are processing these permits and guiding these builders.”

He learned that most permitting mistakes are avoidable, like applying for the wrong zone or forgetting to include a north arrow on an architectural plan. Those oversights can send an application back to square one while clogging up the permitting process for all other projects.

“The wait time disproportionately affects lower margin projects,” Rabah said. “It really constrains the supply of housing, especially the housing we need more of, which is the more affordable kind.”

“I’ve always enjoyed the ‘what if?’ mindset, the clean slate. It’s this way today, but could we imagine it to be something different?”

Govstream’s AI assistants are designed to help first-time builders avoid those errors and make permitting faster for everyone. Rabah and his team began by building what they call an “intelligent intake” platform for a city permitting portal, which guided users through preparing to submit their applications.

When Bellevue first tested Govstream’s intake tool on 276 past residential building permit applications, the city reported a completeness rate of 67%, compared with 22% when those applications were originally filed. According to the company, the latest testing has yielded an 88% completeness rate.

More recently, they’ve begun to build out an AI assistant for the backend, which assists city permit techs with the initial review and reduces what Rabah calls “toil,” like answering unnecessary pre-application emails and tracking down missing documents.

Bellevue staff estimated that Govstream’s tools saved them 152 hours over one month this summer by helping them research and respond to pre-application inquiries.

“For a developer, time is money, so the type of housing that can be built in Bellevue will become more affordable,” said Jake Hesselgesser, Bellevue’s development services director. “This technology has a direct and material impact on the cost of housing.”

Eventually, Govstream.AI will be an end-to-end service, assisting in later stages of the permitting process, too. But Rabah is emphatic that Govstream will not give AI the final say.

“We always put our AI systems in the role of assistants that suggest stuff, but never decide stuff,” Rabah said.

Rabah says Govstream uses preset rules, outside the AI model, to check whether a portion of the application is complete, whether a site needs a geotechnical report, or whether an architect is properly licensed. In Bellevue, city staff retain final authority.

Hesselgesser said that Rabah’s conservative approach to AI is what made the city of Bellevue want to work with his startup.

“Our core principle around Bellevue’s use of AI is to retain human decision making, and we wanted to ensure that we were aligned with a company with the same core value,” Hesselgesser said. “Saf took that holistic approach.”

Around the office, Rabah has become known for his eagerness to build. According to Mariia Derevianko, head of marketing, he spends his weekends building out a product or an idea in order to workshop it with the team.

“He’s very hands-on with the product, with design, marketing, all of the aspects,” Derevianko said. “He never waits for the engineers to build something.”

Most recently, he built a lead tracker to research which cities Govstream should partner with, and previously, he vibe-coded one of the research assistants in the Govstream platform as a template for his software engineers.

Derevianko, who joined the team last year after Rabah poached her from AWS, said he’s also known for his kindness.

“I originally didn’t want to join a start-up,” Derevianko said. “I only said yes because I saw he is a genuinely good person who really cares about this project.”

Govstream.AI has already won at least 12 contracts around the Puget Sound, including King County and the City of Everett, as well as cities across the country, such as Louisville, Kentucky.

Ultimately, Rabah has his eyes set on Seattle, where construction and development has been on the decline. Last December, the city council passed permanent “middle housing” rules to upzone residential neighborhoods and encourage the construction of ADUs, all of which will need a permit.

Seattle tested a competing AI tool from CivCheck in 2025. In June, city staff recommended a pilot that would let applicants check their submissions for completeness before filing.

“We need affordable housing in Seattle,” Rabah said. “We would really, really love to help our home city streamline permitting and remove it as a barrier.”

In founding Govstream.AI, Rabah has found the job he has been looking for: one in which he can build things without the bureaucracy of a large company, all while “doing good.”

“This has become my obsession,” Rabah said. “I can point to things in a city and say, maybe Govstream was a part of what allowed this project to get built.”

Our definition of business isn’t exactly common.

Greater Seattle Partners is the region’s public-private economic development organization uniting business, government, and community leaders to promote Greater Seattle on the global stage. We elevate the region’s story, attract international investment, and build regional economic collaboration to advance inclusive and sustainable economic growth.

Because here, Uncommon Thinkers are always welcome.

#5349. How to Finance Your Business’s Next Stage of Growth

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The right financing strategy funds expansion, balances risk, preserves flexibility, and establishes clear upsides for investors and the company.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Growth can create a real challenge for business leaders. The more successful a company becomes, the more capital it may require to keep growing and maintain or build on that level of success. New customers demand inventory; additional capacity requires equipment; product innovation and expansion into new markets often involve substantial investment before new revenue is realized.

In my role in senior financial leadership, I’ve learned that financing decisions involve both accessing capital and thoughtful strategy. These decisions shape a company’s financial obligations, ownership structure and ability to pursue future opportunities. These decisions also shape the operating model of the company and the future trajectory of the business.

The challenge for companies experiencing growth is determining which combination of internal cash, debt and equity best supports the company’s long-term ambitions. Any decision about capital strategy incorporates tradeoffs.

Before pursuing external financing, leadership teams should examine how effectively their operations generate and retain cash. Improving collections, managing inventory and reinvesting profits can fund expansion without increasing debt or diluting ownership. Many companies leverage a portion of self-financing as a larger part of their capitalization strategy, even a small portion included in a larger debt or equity stake.

Mailchimp demonstrated the potential of this approach, growing without outside equity financing before its acquisition by Intuit in a transaction valued at approximately $12 billion in 2021. Famously, Mailchimp avoided venture capital by prioritizing cash flow and streamlining operations to avoid needing outside capital. In 2020 and 2021, Mailchimp was pushing roughly $300 million in EBITDA.

Self-financing, however, is not equally practical across all industries. A software company with recurring revenue and modest infrastructure requirements has a different capital demand than a manufacturer purchasing machinery or a transportation company expanding its fleet. For asset-heavy businesses, relying exclusively on internal cash may constrain growth and allow competitors to capture emerging opportunities.

The goal is to maximize internal funding while preserving sufficient liquidity to withstand unexpected expenses, delayed payments and economic uncertainty.

Debt and equity represent fundamentally different approaches to financing expansion. Debt creates contractual repayment obligations, while equity exchanges ownership for capital without conventional repayment requirements. Neither approach is better than the other, across the board. Their suitability as financing options depends on the predictability of cash flows, the risks associated with expansion and the company’s long-term objectives.

In equipment finance, financing income-producing assets requires balancing borrowing costs, repayment schedules and anticipated returns. Credit decisions are partially based on these business fundamentals. The same principle applies to businesses investing in production equipment, facilities and other revenue-generating assets. When cash flows are predictable, borrowing can allow owners to retain equity while capturing the financial benefits of expansion. Companies should also recognize that repayment obligations remain even when growth underperforms, potentially restricting liquidity and operational flexibility.

Equity offers an alternative approach for companies developing new technologies, entering uncertain markets or pursuing investments with unpredictable near-term returns. Investors share financial risk and may contribute valuable expertise and connections, but their capital comes at the expense of future ownership and profits. A founder selling 20% of a business may obtain the financing needed to accelerate growth while trading a portion of eventual value.

Investors may also negotiate governance rights, just as lenders may impose financial covenants, something I have considerable experience with in my role as a CFO. Consequently, the true cost of capital extends beyond interest rates and valuation to include the strategic flexibility a company retains. Sometimes, a captive business interest by an individual or institution through equity can supercharge a business through ongoing partnership.

Whether a business is considering relying on cash flow for growth, debt financing or trading equity for capital, the business should consider how much capital the company needs and on what timeline.

An established distributor with predictable demand may use a revolving credit line to finance inventory and receivables, while a company developing an innovative product may require equity to support years of research and market development, like in the biotech industry. In fact, biotech companies can require several years of clinical trial stage development, requiring massive cash runways prior to even conceiving going to market; many of these companies involve acquisitions or exits at maturity.

Many businesses benefit from combining financing sources, using retained earnings for operational improvements, borrowing for established revenue-generating activities and reserving equity for investments involving greater uncertainty.

Capital structures should support corporate strategy rather than dictate it. Businesses should recognize the challenges of dilution and not seek to raise too much capital. The objective is to fund what needs to be funded. The financing strategy that allows the company to pursue growth, withstand setbacks and preserve its ability to create long-term value is the ideal approach for a company making a decision about financing growth.

Growth can create a real challenge for business leaders. The more successful a company becomes, the more capital it may require to keep growing and maintain or build on that level of success. New customers demand inventory; additional capacity requires equipment; product innovation and expansion into new markets often involve substantial investment before new revenue is realized.

In my role in senior financial leadership, I’ve learned that financing decisions involve both accessing capital and thoughtful strategy. These decisions shape a company’s financial obligations, ownership structure and ability to pursue future opportunities. These decisions also shape the operating model of the company and the future trajectory of the business.

The challenge for companies experiencing growth is determining which combination of internal cash, debt and equity best supports the company’s long-term ambitions. Any decision about capital strategy incorporates tradeoffs.

#5348. Electric boat maker Zin Boats raises $5M and launches propulsion business beyond the water

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:58 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:58 am

Zin Boats made a splash with fast, pricey electric boats. But most of its business is now coming from what’s under the floor.

The Seattle startup has launched Zin Power, a new division that will supply its electric propulsion systems to other boat builders and to industries that rely on diesel engines, such as construction and mining.

The company also raised $5 million to scale up production and expanded its headquarters in the Interbay neighborhood to 11,000 square feet.

About 90% of the company’s revenue comes from selling motors and batteries to customers in the marine and drone industries, founder and CEO Piotr Zin told GeekWire. A typical setup includes two motors and about 500 kilowatt-hours of battery storage.

“We noticed a steady demand for pleasure craft year over year, but at the same time a massive increase in propulsion sales,” Zin said.

Customers include StanCraft Wooden Boats, which teamed with Zin on the 340 Hammerhead E, an all-electric wooden runabout. StanCraft delivered the first one to a customer this summer.

GeekWire first checked out the company in early 2024, when it was relaunching after a pandemic shutdown with its Z2R, a 20-foot carbon fiber runabout. Later that year Zin showed off the Z11, a 37-foot electric tender designed to shuttle passengers to and from megayachts at more than 60 mph. The company said boats on the platform would cost $1.75 million to $3.75 million.

The company also offers the Z7 Convertible, a 22-foot runabout with a removable roof that it pitches for fishing, surfing and cruising. The boat has a top speed of 40 mph and a range of more than 80 miles

Zin Power grew out of the drivetrains engineered for those boats. Zin sees the marine track record as a selling point for other industries that need high torque, including construction, mining and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs).

“The ocean is one of the harshest environments there is, so the technology has already proven itself under about the toughest conditions it could face,” Zin said.

Many of those machines still run on diesel engines, a technology more than a century old. Zin said operators are eager to switch to electric.

“What’s interesting is that economics is driving the shift, not regulation or image,” he said.

Electric systems cost up to 70% less to operate, according to Zin. He estimated that replacing a single 250-horsepower industrial diesel engine that runs eight hours a day could save as much as $1.5 million over 10 years.

The new funding will pay for more manufacturing capacity, a dedicated sales and engineering team to work with boat builders, and support for customers converting from diesel. Zin calls it a seed round, with a larger raise planned down the road. The company has raised $6.5 million to date, including a $1.275 million seed round in early 2024.

Zin Boats has nine full-time employees and brings on about a dozen contractors as needed.

For now, each Zin Power system is built to order. The company’s motors range from 100 to 600 kilowatts and deliver up to 2,700 pound-feet of torque, and its systems can run fully electric or as hybrids. A proprietary control unit that Zin Power calls the “Magic Box” manages everything from charging and cooling to software and safety.

“Our goal is to keep delivering what we’ve built while developing simpler, more advanced plug-and-play systems,” Zin said. “Eventually, we want a customer to be able to pull out a diesel engine and drop in a Zin Power system as a direct one-for-one replacement.”

#5347. Crypto News Today: Is Bitcoin Bottoming Out? BTC Bounces Back After PCE Shock

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin bounced back toward $60,000 this morning after news on hotter-than-expected US inflation broke and sent the crypto tumbling to $57,300, its lowest level in more than two years. The rebound has brought back speculation that Bitcoin may finally be approaching a bottom, but ETF outflows and bearish signals continue to cloud the outlook.

October’s Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation came in at 3.8% annually, while core PCE reached 3.3%, above the 3.2% expected by economists. These figures strengthened concerns that the Federal Reserve could keep monetary policy restrictive for longer, which then adds pressure to risk assets like Bitcoin.

Bitcoin nevertheless recovered after briefly dipping below $58,000, as we gauge and predict its next move.

Bitcoin remains down 23% this November, putting it on track for its worst monthly performance since June 2022. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have also suffered nearly $5 billion in net outflows this month through November 24, adding another source of selling pressure.

BlackRock’s IBIT has accounted for more than $4 billion in redemptions during the month, showing how quickly institutional demand has reversed.

However, not all investors are moving in the same direction. Data cited by Nansen shows wallets that rarely move Bitcoin received a net 10,000 BTC from exchanges over the past month, while ETFs collectively sold 70,000 BTC during November.

Nansen data shows large, infrequently moving wallets absorbed a net 10,000 BTC from exchanges over the past month.Meanwhile, spot Bitcoin ETFs sold 70,000 BTC in November.The imbalance is stark. Long term cold wallets are still accumulating, but nowhere near enough to offset…

Bitcoin’s rebound also comes after an arguably huge derivatives-market reset, with leveraged positions being flushed out during the recent slide. That could reduce some immediate selling pressure.

Holders have realized $8.4 billion in net losses over the past 30 days, according to CryptoQuant data, as investors are increasingly capitulating during the selloff. But the figure remains well below the $30 billion recorded during February’s bottom and $18.4 billion during June’s low. Selling pressure has intensified, but the scale of realized losses has yet to match previous capitulation events.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Some analysts believe Bitcoin’s recovery could be running ahead of the underlying market conditions. CoinMarketCap research head Alice Liu warned that the rebound may largely reflect short sellers covering positions, and not fresh demand, leaving prices vulnerable once that buying subsides.

Meanwhile, 10x Research’s bearish signal issued in October correctly anticipated Bitcoin’s decline toward $57,300. The firm has cautioned that oversold conditions can trigger short-term rebounds without necessarily signaling a reversal in the wider trend.

“Bitcoin has reached our $57,300 target. Short-term indicators were oversold for much of the decline, and tactical bounces were always possible. Our market structure work, however, kept pointing to a bearish primary trend.” – 10X Research

Bitcoin faces a difficult combination of persistent ETF withdrawals, uncertain news from Federal Reserve policy, and weakened market sentiment. The selloff has removed substantial leverage, but convincing evidence of renewed demand remains limited.

The $57,300 low is now a key level to defend. Holding that support while ETF outflows begin slowing will likely strengthen the case that Bitcoin is forming a bottom.

#5346. Living Computers closed, but its spirit and vintage machines live on at a museum south of Seattle

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 11:08 amNovember 25, 2026 at 8:16 am

When Seattle’s Living Computers: Museum + Labs closed for good in 2024, it seemed like the end of the line for anyone who wanted to do more than just look at old computers.

But in a Tukwila business park 20 minutes south of downtown, a sizable collection of vintage computers is still alive — kept running by a few of the same people who once did the same for Paul Allen.

The Interim Computer Museum is a nonprofit that opened to the public in 2024 and has quietly grown into a hands-on showcase of dozens of machines, from early Apples and IBM PCs to hulking DEC systems that once filled university labs. At 4,400 square feet of public space, it’s nearly as big as Living Computers was before that museum expanded in 2016.

ICM is led by Stephen Jones, who calls himself the museum’s “caretaker.” Jones spent two decades helping track down and restore machines for Allen, first at PDP Planet, Allen’s private collection of vintage systems, then at Living Computers, where he was senior engineering manager.

When the late Microsoft co-founder’s estate wound down Living Computers, the majority of the collection went to the Mimms Museum of Technology and Art in Georgia, where Jones is also a curator. The machines in Tukwila are privately owned, and Jones has helped bankroll ICM with personal funds, with plans to eventually donate the collection to the nonprofit.

The Mimms museum now holds the Living Computers trademark and has granted ICM “legacy use” of the name, but Jones said he didn’t want to revive it as ICM’s own because “it has a finite past.” Instead, he wants to carry on “the spirit of the engineering focus.”

“Between Mimms and here, this is the legacy,” Jones said. “We show the name and the connection to the past, but we’re doing new things.”

ICM occupies space in Seattle Exchange @ Southcenter, a sprawl of low-slung flex buildings off Strander Boulevard near Westfield Southcenter mall. Its neighbors include a car detailer, a pest control company, a welding shop, an embroiderer and an upholsterer.

More than four decades ago, Seattle Computer Products operated just down Industry Drive. That’s where Tim Paterson wrote 86-DOS, the operating system Microsoft bought and turned into MS-DOS for IBM’s first PC.

Jones calls that proximity part of the “magic” of the location. The museum has a Gazelle computer that SCP built nearby, using boards that Jones said the company hired high school students to assemble and test. Volunteers recently pulled data off its hard drive, which boots into MS-DOS 2.11 and still holds SCP’s own source code.

Allen’s fingerprints are everywhere. One display holds a 1971 letter from Hellmut Golde, director of the University of Washington’s Computer Science Laboratory, kicking Allen and his “friends from the Lakeside School” out of the lab. Among the offenses: tying up the teletypes to print “endless listings,” and taking an acoustic coupler from a professor’s office “without leaving at least a note.” Golde asked them to turn in their keys.

The letter sits beside an Imlac PDS-1, the same type of graphics computer Golde scolded the teens for using without permission. More than five decades later, the letter is headed back to campus: ICM plans to display it, along with the Imlac, at UW’s 60th anniversary celebration for its computer science program in March.

Jones recalled that Allen insisted visitors to Living Computers get “the 10-minute experience” of loading an Altair 8800 from paper tape, just as he remembered it. The kit computer was the machine for which Allen and Bill Gates wrote Microsoft’s first product, and Allen wanted to reinforce “how far we’ve come and how difficult old computers were.” ICM has an Altair 8800 on display.

Around the corner is Miss Piggy, a DEC datasystem 570 that Microsoft used in the early 1980s to support the group that built Multiplan, Word and later Excel. It was also the email host for much of the company, including Gates, who once had to print out an important message on its console printer when the system went down before a speaking engagement.

Recovered email shows Allen pushing to get Piggy networked. “Paul Allen is very keen on doing this,” Henry Burgess wrote in 1982. Retired in 1986, the machine now runs again in Tukwila. It’s one of ICM’s most popular remote systems, and some fans come in just to write programs while sitting next to it.

Other local ties include a PDP-7 that Boeing used to process flight data in the 1960s, and a Toad-1, a modern take on the PDP-10 built in the 1990s by Redmond’s XKL. Jones first got involved with Allen’s world through a 1997 Usenet post inviting PDP-10 enthusiasts onto a Toad. That machine became the cornerstone of PDP Planet.

In a 2024 video for Christie’s, Jones said what inspired Allen was “being able to recover old programs, mythical code, and get them running on hardware so that they can be studied.”

Asked what Allen would make of ICM, Jones didn’t hesitate. “I think he’d be happy,” he said.

On a monitor beside ICM’s PDP-6, a 1968 artificial intelligence program is having trouble.

“SORRY, I DON’T KNOW THE WORD ‘STEEPLE,'” it replies.

The program is SHRDLU, created by Terry Winograd at the MIT AI Lab. It let a user type plain-English commands to move blocks around a virtual world. Only the PDP-6’s front console and display survived, so ICM is rebuilding the machine as a “hybrid,” with the original hardware wired to an emulator.

Jones sees a lesson in that old error message. “You look at this and you think of how we use ChatGPT now,” he said. “The cool thing about SHRDLU is that it can tell you ‘I don’t know.’ It doesn’t try to fabricate anything.”

ICM has its own ties to the modern AI world. An Anthropic employee is a member and strong supporter, and in October the museum brought six vintage computing stations to an Anthropic event, where the company’s Claude chatbot wrote programs for machines like the Commodore 64.

Back in Tukwila, Claude has become one of ICM’s most useful restoration tools. The team feeds it huge stacks of scanned documentation, such as the full set of schematics for a PDP-10. When a machine has a logic fault, they ask where to look, and Claude points them to a page in the maintenance manual or a likely bad module.

“That’s turned things that would take a couple of weeks to solve into a couple of days,” Jones said.

AI can point the way, but the repairs remain hands-on work. When Miss Piggy wouldn’t run properly this year, former Living Computers engineer Josh Dersch stepped through the machine’s microcode one instruction at a time using a recreated DEC test board, until he found a single bad chip. A spare board brought it back.

Asked if it still takes a human to keep these machines running, Jones agreed — at least for now. If a humanoid robot with AI built in ever shows up to do the repairs, he joked, “then I sit at the front desk all day.”

Nearly everything at ICM is meant to be touched, switched on and played with, and that can be intimidating. On machines with nothing but a text prompt, “you kind of have to know the commands in your head already,” Jones said.

That’s by design. From the start, the idea was to challenge people “either by confronting them with their past or demonstrating how difficult it was,” Jones said. His example: two friends, one with an Apple IIe and one with an IBM PC, whose computers “could never share” software. ICM continues that legacy, he said, “challenging the visitor to go beyond what they might feel comfortable with.”

Volunteers have written cheat sheets to help newcomers, and Jones is encouraged when families come in and kids start typing BASIC programs. “That to me was the spirit of what PDP Planet and Living Computers was meant to be,” he said.

Very little is behind glass. Jones jokes that a Timex Sinclair 1000, which would wipe your painstakingly typed program if you bumped it, is “the only computer that deserves to be behind glass.” The goal, he said, is to avoid “a boneyard that people walk through.”

Other highlights include Galaxy Game, the first coin-operated video game, installed at Stanford in 1971 and now being restored, and a Thinking Machines CM-2 supercomputer, whose 40th anniversary ICM just celebrated with members of its original design team.

For younger engineers raised on modern tools, Jones has a go-to move. He asks if they’ve used Linux, then walks them over to the PDP-7, the type of machine Unix was first written on more than 50 years ago. Many of the basic commands they type every day started there.

The collection totals about 6,000 artifacts. Volunteers are also slowly working through roughly 3,000 magnetic tapes and disk packs from Living Computers’ software preservation program. And ICM keeps 32 historic systems online, where members can log in from anywhere to use vintage operating systems, programming languages and games.

That remote access helps explain why ICM has about 500 members and sponsors, even though only 81 members have visited in person this year. Memberships start at $36 a year. Along with a King County grant through 4Culture, they help cover rent, with personal funds from Jones filling the gap. The museum hopes to become self-sustaining within five years, and maybe someday buy its own building.

The museum’s name reflects the urgency. “We’re in this magic window right now, where the hardware can still run, we can still maintain it, you can replace parts,” Jones said. “But slowly we’re getting further and further away.”

ICM is open Saturdays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Admission is $9 for adults and free for those under 18. Last May, the museum revived Vintage Computer Festival Pacific Northwest, which had been canceled in March 2020. The event drew 981 people, and it returns May 1–2 at the Tukwila Community Center.

Among the machines on the floor is MIT-AI, a DECsystem-2020 that once served as the ARPANET host for MIT’s Artificial Intelligence Lab. As Living Computers shut down in 2024, Christopher Zach, who sold the machine to Allen, told GeekWire he was ready to drive a U-Haul to Seattle to rescue it.

When a friend of Zach’s stopped by ICM’s booth at WorldCon and asked about “Chris’s computer,” Jones had a simple message to pass along: “Please just tell him it’s safe.”

#5345. More art, less artificial: Seattle Art Museum billboards troll tech ads and tell people to look up

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 1:27 pmNovember 24, 2026 at 2:04 pm

A billboard taking a swipe at Anthropic’s Claude might sound like the work of a rival AI company. This one is from the Seattle Art Museum.

“The only Claude you need is Monet,” the sign reads. It’s part of the latest wave of messages in SAM’s “Dear Seattle” campaign, which has spent the fall urging people to look up from their screens and see something in person.

Earlier billboards around the city told passersby to “come stare at something that isn’t your inbox” and noted that “even the algorithm thinks you should get out more.” The final batch pushes the AI jokes further, including one asking for “a little more art and a little less artificial” and another promising, “Your phone doesn’t have to know.”

Tech billboards are a fixture in the San Francisco Bay Area, where AI startups cover Highway 101 and city streets with ads that often mean little to anyone outside the industry.

They’re less common around Seattle. Anthropic put up a big orange Claude billboard over Aurora Avenue in 2024, and this spring Bellevue startup Summation put one up along SR 520 because “startup energy should be more visible around here,” its CEO told GeekWire.

“In a city where so much of our lives happens on screens, we’re making a playful case for the things you can only experience in person,” Kat Bryant Flaherty, SAM’s director of communications, said in a statement. She listed “the scale and texture of an artwork, a film with a room full of strangers, making something with your hands, or catching up with a friend over a meal.”

The campaign is tied to changes at the downtown museum itself, where SAM is adding more public space and more reasons to linger, including hands-on art making and music in the Studio at SAM and the newly opened Bar Dojo restaurant.

The campaign runs through the end of the year, with more than 200 ads across the region — more than 20 billboards plus spots on light rail and digital kiosks.

SAM’s campaign is about the same size as the one Bellevue startup Statsig ran in the Bay Area in 2024, with more than 200 billboards and transit posters, but pointed in the opposite direction.

SAM is offering buy-one-get-one-free tickets in December with the code “LOVESAM,” good at both the downtown museum and the Seattle Asian Art Museum in Volunteer Park, to encourage people to visit together.

“We’re hoping to grab attention, spark curiosity, and remind Seattle that there’s a lot happening at SAM worth leaving the house for,” Flaherty said.

#5344. Stop Building AI Into Your Product. Let Your Customers Bring Their Own.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Your B2B customers already pay for an AI assistant. “Bring your own agent” lets you plug into it instead of competing with it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Over the past two years, almost every software company has felt the same pressure: Add AI to the product, or look outdated. So we all did. Chat panels appeared in the corner of every dashboard. “Summarize with AI” buttons showed up next to every text field. Pricing pages grew a new line item for AI credits.

I run a company that makes help desk software for businesses, and we went through this too. But somewhere along the way, I noticed something about our customers that changed how I think about the whole question.

If you sell to businesses, look at what your customers’ employees have open on their screens. Very often it’s a corporate Claude or ChatGPT subscription, or Microsoft 365 Copilot bundled into the Office licenses the company was paying for anyway. Someone in IT or finance evaluated it, signed a contract, went through a security review and rolled it out.

That assistant is becoming the company’s “at-home AI.” It’s the one employees are trained on, the one legal has approved, and increasingly, the one that has context about the business: documents, email, meeting notes, internal wikis. Every company will have one eventually. Frankly, most already do.

Now imagine that same company uses eight or 10 business tools, and each of those vendors has bolted on its own AI assistant. Each one has a different interface, different limits and different data policies. None of them know what the others know. The help desk AI has no idea what was discussed in the CRM, and the CRM’s AI can’t see the project tracker.

That’s not a better workplace. It’s AI sprawl, and it’s the opposite of what the customer wants.

The alternative is simple: Instead of building an assistant into your product, make your product easy for the customer’s existing assistant to use. Let them bring their own agent.

If that phrase sounds familiar, it should. A decade ago, “bring your own device” (BYOD) changed how companies thought about laptops and phones. More recently, “bring your own key” (BYOK) let customers plug their own AI provider’s API key into software instead of paying the vendor for AI usage. Bring your own agent (BYOA) is the next step: The customer doesn’t just bring the key; they bring the whole assistant, with its context, its permissions and its security approvals already in place.

For the customer, the benefits are obvious. They use a tool they already pay for and already know. Their assistant can combine data from your product with everything else it has access to. Asking “which of our biggest accounts filed support tickets this week, and what did we promise them in the last renewal call?” only works if one assistant can see both the help desk and the meeting notes.

For the vendor, the benefits are less obvious but just as real.

You stay out of the token-reselling business: When you build AI features on top of a model provider, you’re effectively buying compute wholesale and reselling it. Your costs grow with usage, your margins depend on someone else’s pricing changes, and you end up designing credit systems and usage caps instead of building your actual product. With BYOA, the customer’s AI subscription covers the compute. Your product provides the data and the actions.

You stop competing with companies that spend billions on models: No software vendor of normal size is going to build a better general-purpose assistant than the frontier AI labs. Trying to match them feature for feature is a losing race. Being the best tool their assistant can connect to is a race you can actually win.

It clarifies product decisions: This one surprised me the most. Once you accept that the customer’s assistant will handle the conversation, the question shifts from “What AI features should we build?” to “What can our product do, and how cleanly can we expose it?” That’s a much healthier question. It pushes you to make your core functionality solid, well-structured and well-permissioned, which is good for every user, not just the ones using AI.

It’s a marketing channel, too: This is the least obvious benefit. AI clients now have their own connector directories, and there’s a growing number of independent MCP registries and listing sites. Getting listed puts your product in front of people at the exact moment they’re looking for tools to connect to their assistant. It’s a new distribution channel, it’s still relatively uncrowded, and it costs you nothing beyond the integration you were building anyway.

This doesn’t mean built-in AI has no place. Some features, such as automatic ticket categorization that runs in the background without anyone asking, make sense to keep inside the product. But the conversational assistant, the one people talk to, increasingly belongs to the customer, not to you.

The practical way to do this today is to implement an MCP server for your product. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard that lets AI assistants discover and use tools in external applications. It’s supported by Claude, ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot Studio and a growing list of other clients. You describe what your product can do, such as search records, create items or update statuses, and any compatible assistant can use those actions on the user’s behalf, within that user’s existing permissions.

There are two common ways to ship an MCP server, and the choice matters more than it seems.

1. A hosted endpoint over HTTP: Your product exposes an MCP endpoint on its own servers, using the protocol’s streamable HTTP transport. The customer adds a URL to their assistant, signs in, and that’s it. Nothing gets installed. When you add new capabilities or fix a bug, every customer gets the update immediately, because there’s only one version: the one you’re running.

2. A local package. You publish a command-line tool or npm package that runs on the user’s machine and talks to your API. This was the common approach early on, and it still works for individual developers.

I strongly recommend the first option. We started with both at my company, and we’re now phasing out the local package. Each installed copy is a version you can’t update, and customers running old packages kept missing newer features.

But the bigger reason is security. Large organizations increasingly won’t allow third-party code to run on employee machines, and for good reason. The past couple of years have brought a steady stream of critical-severity vulnerabilities and software supply chain attacks, including compromised packages in the npm ecosystem itself. Asking a security team to approve a package that runs locally with access to company data is a hard sell. Asking them to approve an HTTPS endpoint on a vendor they’ve already vetted is a much easier conversation.

A hosted endpoint also fits how companies roll out AI. Organization-wide connectors in enterprise AI plans are typically set up once by an administrator and then made available to everyone. Support OAuth sign-in so each employee connects with their own account and permissions, and you’ve removed most of the friction.

It’s tempting to view the customer’s AI assistant as a competitor for attention. If people spend their day in Claude or Copilot, won’t they spend less time in your product?

Maybe. But they were going to use that assistant anyway. The real question is whether it can reach your product when they need it. If it can’t, you’re the tool that gets worked around. If it can, you’re part of how the company works.

B2B buyers don’t want another AI. They want the one they already have to work with everything else they pay for. Build for that.

Over the past two years, almost every software company has felt the same pressure: Add AI to the product, or look outdated. So we all did. Chat panels appeared in the corner of every dashboard. “Summarize with AI” buttons showed up next to every text field. Pricing pages grew a new line item for AI credits.

I run a company that makes help desk software for businesses, and we went through this too. But somewhere along the way, I noticed something about our customers that changed how I think about the whole question.

#5343. A Bigger Business Isn’t Automatically a Better One. Here’s What to Ask Before Scaling.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Scaling a business isn’t just about hiring more people and increasing revenue. Growth brings new management challenges, operational complexity and the risk of losing sight of customers.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’ve spent 13 years building a business. It’s long enough to figure out what works, and definitely long enough to get a lot of things wrong. When we were five people in a 300-square-foot office, our team tripled in size in a year. Our client base and revenue grew just as quickly. At some point, I genuinely started to believe we were the gods of consulting. As it turned out, we were simply very good at running a small company.

That is one of the lovely things about early success. It gives you confidence and the impression that you have figured out the whole business. Now that I’ve had time to reflect, I see that the first lesson of scaling is that success at one stage doesn’t automatically prepare you for the next.

If a team of five can become 10 by working harder and talking more, it’s tempting to assume that 10 can become 50 the same way. But growth is not multiplication. A company of eight people and a company of 30 are not the same business at different sizes. They are two different organizations that require two different ways of managing.

In its early days, a small company can get by on instinct, proximity and a good deal of improvisation just because, as a founder, you are involved in nearly everything. You know the clients, notice the work, answer questions and make decisions often before anyone has had time to schedule a meeting about them.

For me, the hardest part wasn’t letting go of tasks. It was realizing that the quality of my business now depended on decisions I wasn’t making, and sometimes didn’t even know were being made.

This is a transition I didn’t handle perfectly. One of my wrong calls was appointing people to management roles because they were excellent specialists. It seemed reasonable at the time, but expertise in consulting doesn’t automatically equip someone to lead a team or resolve a conflict. The difference becomes significant when the business depends on managers to preserve quality without the founder standing nearby.

I am convinced that a company must become less dependent on its founder at precisely the moment the founder may feel most protective of it. That requires more than delegating tasks. I’d say develop leaders who can exercise judgment, establish standards that don’t live solely in the founder’s memory and distribute authority with enough clarity. Without it, founders often remain the final decision-makers, even after building several layers of management.

If you recognize your business in this stage of growth, Ichak Adizes’s model of the company life cycle offers a useful way to understand this transition. The entrepreneurial “Go-Go” stage, with its energy and instinct for opportunity, eventually gives way to “Adolescence,” when informal habits must yield to professional management and clearer authority.

These growing pains don’t necessarily mean you’re running a bad business. On the contrary, they may simply mean you’ve outgrown the way you used to run it. This model gives founders a way to understand why the habits that helped a young company move quickly may no longer serve the organization as it grows.

One of the easiest traps to fall into when scaling is that you can become so busy building the company that you forget who you’re building it for. You can look at your dashboard, see rising revenue and new sign-ups, and think you’re winning. Meanwhile, right under your nose, the quality your loyal clients are getting is quietly tanking.

It’s incredibly easy to lose sight of the customer when your calendar is consumed by recruitment and endless alignments. You end up stuck in back-to-back meetings talking about structure, while your actual clients are dealing with junior staff who don’t fully understand their business yet.

Ask yourself, when was the last time you personally spoke to a client not to sell them something, but to understand whether your company is still delivering the value they expect?

As a business grows, the cost of complexity grows with it. More employees mean more coordination, more management responsibilities and more opportunities for processes to break down. Before committing to another expansion push, it’s worth looking at the reality of the market.

OECD figures show that among SMEs with 10 to 249 employees, 8% to 14% qualified as employment scalers in 2020, while 12% to 24% qualified as turnover scalers. The OECD also found that scalers were, on average, 20% more productive than other SMEs before their high-growth phase, with that advantage rising to 35% after three years.

What this reinforces for me is that expansion should never be an automatic next step. I try to keep that question front and center; otherwise, you can become so absorbed in perfecting the company’s internal structure that you stop thinking about the actual person using your product.

So before the next growth effort, make sure you do not scale chaos:

Not every business needs to become bigger. Sometimes scaling creates value. Sometimes it simply creates overhead. More employees do not automatically mean more success. More markets do not automatically mean more opportunities. And higher revenue does not necessarily mean a healthier business.

In specialist consulting, a focused team of 10 can be more profitable and resilient than an organization of 50. In fintech, entering another country may be strategically sound, or it may add cost and complexity without improving the customer proposition.

When we were five people in that small office, I thought learning to make money meant I knew how to build a big business. It took me 13 years to realize that building a bigger company and building a better company are not the same thing.

I’ve spent 13 years building a business. It’s long enough to figure out what works, and definitely long enough to get a lot of things wrong. When we were five people in a 300-square-foot office, our team tripled in size in a year. Our client base and revenue grew just as quickly. At some point, I genuinely started to believe we were the gods of consulting. As it turned out, we were simply very good at running a small company.

That is one of the lovely things about early success. It gives you confidence and the impression that you have figured out the whole business. Now that I’ve had time to reflect, I see that the first lesson of scaling is that success at one stage doesn’t automatically prepare you for the next.

If a team of five can become 10 by working harder and talking more, it’s tempting to assume that 10 can become 50 the same way. But growth is not multiplication. A company of eight people and a company of 30 are not the same business at different sizes. They are two different organizations that require two different ways of managing.

#5342. Meta’s teen restrictions have a gap: TikTok, Snapchat and YouTube leave teens room to scroll

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 25, 2026 at 8:21 am

Meta’s new teen restrictions, set to take effect by late February, could meaningfully curb endless scrolling. A new study suggests they probably won’t.

That’s because the restrictions, which are part of a settlement between Meta and dozens of attorneys general, including Washington’s, apply only to Instagram and Facebook. They leave out Snapchat, TikTok and Google-owned YouTube.

“The simple workaround right now is that you just switch platforms, and we already know that teens are on three to four platforms on average,” said Dr. Dimitri Christakis, a principal investigator at the Center for Child Health, Behavior and Development at Seattle Children’s.

Christakis led research published Wednesday showing Instagram and Facebook accounted for roughly 20% of total daily social media use for youth. So when the restrictions kick in, teens could just shift to other platforms.

The rules establish a two-hour daily limit combined across Instagram and Facebook, restrict access to content from midnight to 6 a.m., and mute most school-hour push notifications. Parents can adjust the protections, and direct messaging is exempt.

If the same limits were applied across the five most popular platforms, that could make a dent in teen usage, according to the research letter in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

In an analysis of recorded app activity from 1,803 adolescent Android users, the researchers estimated:

The study has no way of knowing how teens will respond to the restrictions or the impacts on their health. It simply estimates how much previously recorded activity would fall under the rules.

The researchers disclosed ties to social media litigation. Christakis reported paid legal consulting work, including for Washington’s attorney general, and co-author Lauren Hale of Stony Brook University reported fees for serving as an expert witness. The third author is Yihong Zhao of Columbia University.

Despite the limited benefits of the coming restrictions, Christakis said they’re a “step in the right direction.”

“Let’s say it’s an incremental improvement. It’s clearly not going to be enough by itself because of what our study found,” he said. “But these are the right kinds of restrictions. We need to make them universal, and we need to enforce them.”

Meta, not surprisingly, is in favor of having the restrictions apply industry wide.

When the settlement was announced in August the company issued a statement saying that “ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative.”

Meta called on others to do the same: “For meaningful progress to happen, we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard…”

The agreement resolves claims by 48 states, Washington, D.C., and U.S. territories that Meta designed addictive platforms and failed to protect young users, among other allegations. Meta did not admit wrongdoing.

In addition to the safety changes, Meta agreed to pay participating governments up to $17.1 billion over a decade, according to Washington’s attorney general. Washington will receive at least $237 million and could receive nearly $339 million.

The higher settlement is unlocked only if TikTok and YouTube adopt similar protections and make payments of their own, according to Meta. If that happens, additional restrictions kick in, curbing access on all the platforms from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m.

Those additional hours are significant. The researchers found nearly as much use between 10 p.m. and midnight as during the entire midnight-to-6-a.m. window covered by the initial limits.

Whether the other companies will follow remains unclear. All five social media platforms are named in additional legal challenges alleging harm to youth, Reuters reported, including suits filed by individuals, school districts and municipalities.

In September, TikTok reached its first settlement in a state-led case, agreeing to teen usage restrictions in Alabama and a payment of at least $100 million, according to Reuters. YouTube CEO Neal Mohan, meanwhile, dismissed joining Meta’s agreement and emphasized his company’s own safety efforts, CNN reported.

Christakis said both time spent on social media and the platforms’ features can exacerbate problems involving sleep, mental health, body image and attention. He hopes the growing body of research translates into action.

“I’m not a legislator, and I’m not an advocate. I’m a scientist that’s really trying to make sure that we apply science in the best interests of our children’s health,” he said. “And in this space, in particular, we haven’t been doing that.”
