#5340. ‘Positive Charge’ season finale: What we learned chasing climate solutions across eight episodes

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:10 amNovember 25, 2026 at 9:11 am

Editor’s note: GeekWire reporter Lisa Stiffler, who covers climate and sustainability, co-hosts the Positive Charge podcast with producer Laura Scott.

We went inside a fusion lab in Everett, a jet fuel plant in Moses Lake and a factory in British Columbia giving old EV batteries a second life. We tasted plant-based chicken nuggets at 9 a.m. and stepped into a shipping container in Tacoma that destroys “forever chemicals.”

Over eight episodes, the inaugural season of the Positive Charge podcast from GeekWire went across the Pacific Northwest (and beyond) in search of promising climate and sustainability technologies to help humanity dig our way out of some pretty dire environmental straits.

While the challenge is huge — a warming planet, increased use of fossil fuels, toxic chemicals in our food and water — there are wide-ranging solutions out there, and many are taking hold.

On this episode, GeekWire co-founder Todd Bishop sits down with producer Laura Scott and me, the hosts of Positive Charge, to look back on the season. We explore the themes that emerged across the episodes, savor some highlights and even get a little emotional when discussing the question of whether all of it left us more hopeful about the planet.

Going behind the scenes. At Helion Energy in Everett, we got a sneak peek of a miniaturized fusion test device that was cordoned off and still under construction. To see it, we walked behind a huge plastic curtain, which Laura memorably compared to walking into the Costco dairy section.

Our podcast on alternative proteins went inside Rebellyous Foods, a startup manufacturing plant-based chicken nuggets being served in U.S. schools, as well as some medical and correctional facilities. We were offered a plate of the nuggets — which we scarfed down, despite the tour taking place first thing in the morning.

“My biggest regret of the whole season,” Laura said, “is that we did not take Rebellyous up on their offer to send us home with those chicken nuggets because you cannot buy them in stores.”

The importance of large, committed customers. A lot of these technologies are expensive propositions, from R&D to prototypes to scaling. “Having a willing and able corporate buyer is something that can really spark the innovation to happen,” Todd observed.

That includes Microsoft’s agreement to buy power from Helion, purchase agreements for sustainable aviation fuel from Twelve and Montana Renewables, and Redwood Materials‘ deal to supply used EV batteries to power a data center for Crusoe. Rebellyous built its business on school lunch programs.

The essential role of organizations coming together collectively to support new sustainable technologies was a key message of a New York Climate Week panel, where I interviewed Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, and Jason Knauf, CEO of The Earthshot Prize.

We discussed the fact that when customers commit, it unlocks investments to scale production. That in turn lowers costs for everything from faux nuggets to cleaner jet fuel.

AI is driving the money. The data centers behind the AI boom are often cast as a threat to tech companies’ climate goals. In several episodes, they were also a reason for money to flow into clean energy.

“There’s so much money going into environmental solutions because of data centers,” Laura said. “It’s a catalyst for funding. It’s a catalyst for fusion.”

There’s money to be made. While many sustainability entrepreneurs are fundamentally mission-driven, they’re also focused on the fiscal bottom line and so are venture capitalists.

At Pacific Northwest Climate Week, Laura was struck by how enthusiastic investors are about the space, and not only because they want to save the planet. They’re “entirely self-interested,” she said, “and that’s what gave me hope.”

PNW is a sustainability hub. In each episode of Positive Charge, we toured a Pacific Northwest startup, plus we interviewed related companies outside the area and sector experts.

The local companies included Helion and Zap Energy in Everett, Aquagga in Tacoma, Sedron Technologies in Sedro-Woolley, Twelve in Moses Lake, Rebellyous in Seattle and Moment Energy in British Columbia.

The range of topics reinforced the region’s standing as a hub for sustainable tech, including batteries, fusion, aviation, environmental cleanup, and even potentially overlooked fields, such as end-of-life services.

Laura’s unexpected favorite episode was about startups offering human composting as a green alternative to burial or cremation, and Todd ranked it a close second (his No. 1 was EV battery reuse).

Seattle is home to Recompose — the first U.S. company to offer the service after its founder, Katrina Spade, spearheaded the effort in 2019 to make the practice legal. Since then, human composting startups Return Home and Earth Funeral have also launched in the Seattle area.

After exploring all of these technologies and talking to entrepreneurs, investors and leaders in the space, Todd asked if we were more or less hopeful for the planet.

“Definitely more hopeful,” Laura said. “I didn’t expect to feel more hopeful, though. I expected to feel about the same, or maybe a little bit worse.”

But seeing the financial case for these solutions helped shift her thinking. One example is Sedron, which is treating sewage waste with a technology that destroys PFAS forever chemicals and also generates enough clean electricity that the excess can be sold to others. Laura was impressed by the opportunity to do right by the environment while creating revenue.

I hover between hope and anxiety. But after years of covering these issues, I appreciated a sentiment shared by Earthshot finalist Franco Rodríguez Viau, CEO and co-founder of Satellites on Fire, who said he needs to do everything he can to tackle climate change, whether or not humanity succeeds in reaching its goals.

That’s how I feel about covering climate. As I mentioned on the show, I don’t know if I feel hopeful, “but I can’t feel indifferent. I have to show up and do this.”

Positive Charge is a GeekWire podcast sponsored by Amazon Sustainability.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5339. Etzioni on AI: 18 ways to use AI this Thanksgiving

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:17 amNovember 25, 2026 at 10:16 am

Here are 18 creative ways to use AI this Thanksgiving. Some save you time in the kitchen or at the airport, and others aim to make the meal more fun. The don’ts at the end could save your turkey, and my very last suggestion is perhaps the best.

Flight delay forecasting. Apps like Flighty (start with free tier) use machine learning to predict whether your flight will leave on time and why it might not.

Cancellation playbook drafted in advance. Have the backup flights and a rebooking script ready ahead of time, so a cancellation means consulting your AI instead of starting from scratch.

Airport pickup routing. Five relatives land at different times at two airports, and AI works out who drives whom. It can even send a polite request on your behalf.

A personal travel agent. Vayo (free, private beta), a new Seattle startup co-founded by my friend Mike Fridgen, connects to your inbox and pulls in your flight, hotel and restaurant confirmations. It keeps an eye on them for price drops and changes.

Oven Tetris. Give it your oven’s size, every dish’s temperature and the serving time. It works backward to a minute-by-minute schedule and flags the conflicts.

Decoding grandma’s recipe card. Photograph the card and have AI modernize it under one rule: it never invents quantities. “A pinch” stays “a pinch.” “un poco” or “ein bissl” may be translated, but not changed.

Reconstructing a lost dish. Several relatives describe a dish a late grandparent made. AI triangulates a recipe, you cook test versions, and the family votes on which one tastes right.

Pairing from the wines on hand. AI picks from bottles you actually own, and those brought over by guests, dish by dish, instead of a generic list. Last-minute fun!

Potluck dispatcher. One AI thread collects RSVPs and dish claims so you don’t end up with four green bean casseroles.

Trivia built from your own family’s facts. ChatGPT can now run it as a playable game, with answer buttons and a running score inside the conversation.

AI-prepped grandparent interview. Feed the AI what you already know and have it draft questions about the gaps. Record it, and afterward AI turns the transcript into a short illustrated booklet that’s in the mail by Christmas.

Angry Uncle rehearsal. Karin Tamerius, a political psychiatrist, built the Angry Uncle Bot, and it still runs in ChatGPT. A coach asks for your issue and your stance. You set the uncle’s temper from Annoyed to Apoplectic and choose whether he’s drunk or sober, and the coach critiques each reply before he answers.

Live interpreter for multilingual families. Put ChatGPT’s voice mode (paid plans) in the middle of the table so the great-aunt who only speaks Hebrew or Spanish is part of the conversation instead of watching it.

Friday leftover remix. Photograph the fridge and get a menu that makes Friday’s leftovers feel like a new meal.

Specific thank-you notes. Each note names what that person actually brought or said.

Photo triage. AI picks the best 20 of 400 photos and captions them in the family’s inside-joke voice.

“We missed you” letter for someone who wasn’t at the table. AI drafts it from the stories told at dinner.

Black Friday skeptic. Before you buy, check Google’s price insights, which tells you whether a price is high, low or typical for the past three months. Last year, 36% of Black Friday items showed no savings over their prices a few weeks earlier. Better yet, set a price track and let Google’s agent buy the item at eligible U.S. stores when it hits your number, after you confirm.

I consider myself an OG Black Friday skeptic. Back in 2011, I told the New York Times (gift link) that after crunching the price data at my startup Decide.com, the lowest electronics prices usually came in early December, not on Black Friday.

Don’t trust an AI turkey recipe on its own. Back in 2022, when the New York Times cooked a Thanksgiving from GPT-3 recipes, the turkey recipe called for one garlic clove for a 12-pound bird and no butter or oil. It came out dry and flavorless.

Don’t take a chatbot’s word on an airline’s rules. Air Canada’s chatbot told a grieving passenger he could claim a bereavement discount after he flew. The real policy said no, and he had to take the airline to a tribunal to collect $812 (Canadian). Check the airline’s own policy page, and screenshot what the bot tells you.

Don’t click on the deal of the century. Scammers now use AI to make fake shopping sites look legitimate, and the number of fake sites jumped 250% last holiday season, according to NordVPN. Type the retailer’s address yourself.

Don’t try to win the family argument with AI-fetched facts. Even the creator of Angry Uncle Bot says that bombarding your uncle with facts only makes him angrier. Ask questions and listen instead.

Here’s another option: give technology a rest.

Unplug from your devices and from AI, and have an AI-free, 100% human Thanksgiving.

#5337. FCC clears SpaceX to put up to a million satellites in orbit for Starmind data center network

by Alan Boyle on Nov 25, 2026 at 4:46 pmNovember 25, 2026 at 4:48 pm

The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to send up to a million satellites into orbit for its Starmind data-processing network.

In a news release, the FCC touted today’s decision as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space” and echoed the high-flown language that SpaceX used to describe the network in its application 10 months ago.

“It promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization — one that can harness the full power of the sun,” the agency said.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the plan “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

Carr signaled that he was all in on the Trump administration’s support for rapid data center expansion, despite a growing backlash that figured in this month’s midterm elections. He said that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership” in artificial intelligence.

“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” Carr said.

In a post to X, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk told Carr that his praise was “much appreciated.”

“This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk said.

Proponents of solar-powered orbital data centers say such constellations will address the top concerns about terrestrial data centers, including land use, power consumption and water requirements for cooling. Critics point to the engineering challenges, including concerns about cooling the satellites, managing space traffic and dealing with orbital debris.

In approving SpaceX’s application, the FCC rejected opposition from Amazon and Viasat, as well as from the American Astronomical Society, which raised concerns about the constellation’s impact on the night sky. The AAS said in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision.

The FCC attached several conditions to its authorization, including requirements for communications backups, regular updates and a detailed plan for orbital debris mitigation.

SpaceX was cleared to operate its satellites at orbits ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (310 to 623 miles) in altitude. The first satellite is to be put into operation no later than 2033, and the FCC calls for the full constellation to be operating by 2040.

In August, SpaceX announced that it was partnering with Nvidia to design the compute payload for the Starmind AI1 satellite. “Each of the Starmind satellites will include Nvidia Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs for datacenter-class space compute,” SpaceX said at the time.

SpaceX’s facility in Redmond, Wash., makes the satellites for the Starlink telecommunications network — but in a filing related to this year’s initial public offering, SpaceX said its operation in Bastrop, Texas, would be put in charge of producing AI compute satellites.

The FCC said it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals and intends to issue decisions on each proposal “according to the agency’s regular procedures.”

#5336. ‘Aether & Iron’: Seattle-area indie game studio builds a noir detective RPG in the sky

by Thomas Wilde on Nov 26, 2026 at 8:51 amNovember 26, 2026 at 8:51 am

Some video games exist at the confluence point between a surprising number of genres, which can make them difficult to explain to people who aren’t hip-deep in the hobby. That’s why several of the most popular categories are currently nicknamed after the most visible games in them, such as the “Metroidvania” or “Soulslike.” Sure, this isn’t anywhere near the biggest problem in the video game industry at the moment, but we’re going to have to figure this out sooner or later.

Aether & Iron, created by the Issaquah, Wash.-based developer Seismic Squirrel, with co-developer Chaos Theory Games, is at one of those weird genre points. It’s described by its developers as a “narrative RPG,” which works well enough, but that also doesn’t exactly say that much.

It’s worth saying up front that Aether & Iron is on a slow boil. It’s a 30-hour game that unfolds at a careful pace, building out an elaborate science-fiction setting from first principles. If you’re looking for fast thrills, it’s not the experience for you. Instead, think of it like a long novel with points of potential failure, where every opportunity for interactivity is also a chance for you to take its story in a different direction.

Aether & Iron is set in an alternate universe where a strange substance called aether was found beneath Manhattan in 1871. Sixty-seven years later, the study and exploitation of aether has become its own branch of science, which led to a great technological leap forward. Much of New York has been transformed into a three-tiered flying city, split between the Lowers, the Uppers and the Heights. The higher a neighborhood flies, the higher its society.

You enter the story in 1938 in the role of Gia Randazzo, a smuggler from the Lowers who’s hit hard times. She’s so desperate for work that she takes a job she shouldn’t, as a driver and bodyguard for a young scientist from the Heights named Eleanor Reinhardt. It should be a milk run, but Dr. Reinhardt has enemies she doesn’t know about.

In short order, an assassin tries to kill them both, someone steals Gia’s car, and she and Dr. Reinhardt end up stuck together in the worst parts of the Lowers. With no money, a loaner vehicle and few friends left, Gia has to figure out who wants Dr. Reinhardt dead and why. That puts her on a collision course with a revolutionary movement, several of New York’s power brokers and a conspiracy that could knock the city back out of the sky.

You could call Aether & Iron something like “airship noir.” Despite its science-fiction trappings, it’s a dark detective novel at heart. Yes, humanity’s built up into the sky, but the street is always the street. Mickey Spillane meets William Gibson.

During dialogue and investigation sequences, Aether & Iron uses a pair of virtual six-sided dice to determine whether you succeed or fail at a given task. As you get further into the game, you can acquire items that let you reroll those dice on a failed check.

More importantly, you earn experience points for accomplishments and victories, which grant you skill points that can be spent in one of nine categories. You can customize Gia to follow several distinct character tracks, such as a detective, a back-alley brawler or a fast-talking con woman. That influences the path you take through the game and the options that become available to you.

No matter how you choose to play Gia, you can’t always avoid a fight. All the combat in Aether & Iron takes place behind the wheel, with Gia and her crew driving customized vehicles. You can acquire a whole fleet of cars and trucks, then kit them out with special weapons, utility devices, armored plates and matching paint jobs.

Each fight consists of a turn-based tactical battle through the streets in and around New York. In addition to simply shooting up an enemy, you can sideswipe them to force them off the road or into other cars.

Many of the city’s thoroughfares are falling apart or prone to sudden lane changes, so most fights will have their own set of additional hazards. Fortunately, they’re as dangerous to your enemies as they are to you, so you can exploit the road hazards if you think fast enough.

If I had to point at one problem I’ve got with Aether & Iron, it might be that the combat has a couple of unlabeled difficulty curves. Specifically, a few fights are built around specific types of damage to such a degree that the only real way past them is to reload an old save and modify all my vehicles for that particular encounter.

If you like the idea of constantly tweaking your vehicle collection for specific combat purposes, like heat shielding or knockback resistance, you’ll have some fun here. If you’re like me and you tend to rely on set-and-forget general-purpose builds, you’ll run into some roadblocks.

Other than that, you might know already whether or not you want to check it out. There’s a lot of care and art in Aether & Iron, mixed with a unique science-fiction setting that isn’t quite like anything else in video games at the moment.

Aether & Iron is currently available for PC and Mac via Steam for $24.99. Seismic Squirrel plans to release the game for PlayStation and Xbox in 2027.

#5335. Startup Spotlight: Aventide builds AI client management software for consultants and coaches

Startup Spotlight profiles tech startups in the Pacific Northwest.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 27, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 25, 2026 at 2:33 pm

Christian Quiver and Eric Baxter met in a grocery store parking lot, introduced by their wives. Quiver needed a designer for a project, so the two swapped numbers and agreed to try working together for 90 days. Four years later, they’re building a startup together in the Columbia River Gorge.

Their startup, Aventide, opened to the public on Oct. 29. It’s AI-powered software for consultants, coaches and others who sell their expertise one client at a time. Aventide drafts proposals, invoices and follow-ups, but nothing goes to a client until the owner approves it.

Eric Baxter, CDO, and Christian Quiver, CEO, Founder

The name blends “abhainn,” the Irish Gaelic word for river, with “tide,” for the spot where a river meets the sea and where towns and ports have long grown up.

Quiver, the CEO, lives in White Salmon, Wash., and spent more than five years at Amazon. He led go-to-market for the in-store experience as Amazon’s device stores grew from two locations to 50. Baxter is chief design officer and lives in nearby Trout Lake. He spent 25 years in product design, including nearly seven years leading user experience at Welocalize, whose clients included Amazon, Google and Apple.

The idea started in 2025 with a question from Baxter’s wife: Which part of his decades of designing products for other people actually brought him joy? His answer was helping people, especially those pushed out by AI-era layoffs who were trying to start something of their own. Quiver bought in that October.

The pair spent more than six months testing with three groups of business owners in the Gorge, including at a demo day in June with the Mid-Columbia Innovation Hub. They kept meeting people who live in small towns and sell their expertise to companies in Seattle or Portland. “A consultant in a small town can land a corporate client,” Quiver said in an email.

The two-person company is bootstrapped and says 81 people are using Aventide so far. After a 14-day free trial, plans cost $39 or $99 a month. Aventide also publishes estimates of the electricity and water behind everyday tasks in the app. Quiver says the figures could be off by a factor of two either way. “If you ask what it costs in electricity and water to use our product, you get a straight answer,” he said.

We caught up with Quiver for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch?

Aventide is an AI-native client management platform for people paid by the session, project or event. It replaces separate booking, proposal, contract, portal and invoice apps, and runs more than one business from one login.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

Tool fragmentation in small client businesses, and the fact that the owner ends up being the human glue holding all of it together.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

That the barrier isn’t price or features. People don’t have time to switch systems, and many aren’t comfortable with their own software stack. So we onboard anyone who wants it one-on-one.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

Everything. It has fundamentally changed what a small team can build and run. We have always worked as experience builders first, and AI lets a team of two think bigger, test faster, and deliver a world-class product that would have taken what seems like 100-200 people just a year or two ago. It cuts our time from idea to execution by at least 50x.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

People hear “AI for small business” and picture a chat box taped onto legacy software. Instead of making you click through old CRM menus with a writing bot on the side, Aventide wires AI directly into your bookings, contracts, portals, and payments so you just say it, review it and approve.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Choosing which problem we wanted to solve. Our original mission was far too vague to build. We set out to help people through the AI era, but the interviews and prototypes kept landing on client services. Following that meant narrowing a big mission into one product for one kind of owner.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Think bigger, and focus on the whole experience you want to create. Outside of a few rare cases, narrow single-purpose tools are old hat now because nobody wants another tab to manage. The future belongs to software where someone can say, “This is my one tool for this category of my life.

50,000 human-scale businesses use Aventide to own their client relationships directly, keeping more money in small businesses and giving more time back to the people running them.

#5334. Seattle skier vibe-codes ‘Pow Pow,’ a new snow report app that doesn’t sugarcoat the conditions

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 27, 2026 at 8:30 amNovember 27, 2026 at 8:30 am

Jeremy Sanford can’t control the weather that will hit ski resorts this winter, but he hopes his new app can at least tell you whether it’s worth loading up the car — or calling in sick.

Sanford, a senior product designer at Microsoft who grew up on the Eastside and has been skiing and snowboarding since he was a kid, has been building Pow Pow on nights and weekends, using “vibe coding” and Claude to do the work he couldn’t do himself.

The free app for iPhone and Android combines forecast data and readings from mountain snow sensors into snow reports for more than 200 resorts, from Snoqualmie Pass to Niseko, Japan.

Each resort gets a 1–5 “Pow Rating,” where a 5 means call in sick, and a blunt one-liner that says whether it really dumped overnight or your powder day is about to turn to rain.

For Sanford, the stakes come with a full car. He has two kids, ages 4 and 7, whom he is teaching to ski.

“I gotta load up the car with the kids and all the gear,” he said. “Is it just gonna be kind of crappy conditions when we get up there?”

He said none of the resort or weather apps he used gave him exactly what he wanted, and he didn’t fully trust the resorts’ numbers.

“You kind of got to take them with a grain of salt, because I feel like they inflate the numbers a little bit,” he said.

With Pow Pow, the aim is “an honest representation of what the conditions are actually like,” Sanford said. For the details, a section called “Nerd stuff” charts snowfall, base depth, snow quality, snow line, wind and UV.

“It’s got six inches of snow overnight, but what else is going on?” he said. “Oh, it’s maybe super wet up there now, and it’s supposed to be raining this afternoon.”

The headlines are where the app shows some attitude. The default version is family friendly, a second setting adds some profanity, and an “Unhinged” mode goes further. On a bluebird day with no new snow, the app might just tell you to “rip the groomers.”

Sanford said weather apps “can get redundant,” and he wanted “to just add a little bit of fun and add personality to it.”

A paid tier, Pow Pro, adds powder alerts, a 14-day outlook, resort webcams inside the app, home-screen widgets and the Unhinged headlines.

“Honestly, it’s a little bit of an experiment,” Sanford said. “If you could make a couple bucks off it on the side, great, but it’s not really the end goal.”

He got the idea in August, when he thought it would be cool to have “a ski app that I actually cared about” — one that looked and felt good.

Sanford has spent his career designing apps, not coding them. After graduating from Seattle Pacific University with a degree in visual communication design, he joined Microsoft in 2012, working on apps that shipped with Windows 8, including Weather, and later on the Microsoft Band. He spent nearly three years as a UX designer at Amazon, based in Edinburgh, Scotland, before returning to Microsoft in 2019. He now works on SharePoint.

“I don’t have a background in coding or engineering, and so there was always kind of like a hump … a barrier to entry,” he said. AI tools were “the unlock for me to actually make something real.”

Claude did much of the heavy lifting. “Claude and I are buddies,” Sanford said.

Next up, he’s experimenting with a feature that would recommend gear based on the day’s conditions, such as a powder board, a darker lens for better visibility, or extra layers if it’s going to get colder in the afternoon. He’s also asking skiers and snowboarders to send feedback through the app.

A good read on conditions could matter more than usual this winter. A very strong El Niño, possibly a record-setter, is building in the Pacific, and NOAA’s outlook favors a warmer-than-normal winter for the Pacific Northwest.

Meteorologist Larry Schick, who writes the Powder Poobah forecast, wrote last month that the season won’t be a bust. But he expects a slow start, with warm early storms and high snow levels, and warned that skiers “may have to pivot quickly and cherry pick” the best days.

Sanford is “cautiously optimistic” about the season. He has seven or eight resorts pinned to his phone’s home screen, webcams included.

“Hopefully this year is decent,” he said. “The last year was not amazing.”

WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann didn’t plan for his family’s control of WeWork to end at his death but instead expected to pass that control to future generations of Neumanns, too, says Business Insider.

The outlet reports that in a speech Neumann gave to employees in January of this year, footage of which it says it has viewed, Neumann is seen saying that WeWork isn’t “just controlled — we’re generationally controlled.” He reportedly goes on to say that while the five children he shares with wife Rebekah Neumann “don’t have to run the company,” they “do have to stay the moral compass of the company.”

According to BI, Neumann even invoked his future grandchildren, telling those gathered: “It’s important that one day, maybe in 100 years, maybe in 300 years, a great-great-granddaughter of mine will walk into that room and say, ‘Hey, you don’t know me; I actually control the place. #5332. Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game

A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.

This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.

Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.

Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.

“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.

“So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”

With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.

“A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.

What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.

Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.

The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.

Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.

Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.

The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.

The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

#5331. Get a reality check on ‘Blade Runner 2099’ and other AI nightmares

BOT or NOT? This special series explores the evolving relationship between humans and machines, examining the ways that robots, artificial intelligence and automation are impacting our work and lives.

by Alan Boyle on Nov 27, 2026 at 10:04 amNovember 27, 2026 at 11:57 am

The year is 2099, and the replicants are in charge.

For decades, humans had been making a mess of things. Eventually, the super-intelligent, super-strong androids that humans created to serve them rebelled. Before the rebellion, humans hunted down rogue replicants. Now the replicants hunt down rogue humans.

That’s the premise for “Blade Runner 2099,” the latest chapter of a sci-fi saga that began in 1968 with Philip K. Dick’s classic noir novel, “Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?” The tale made the leap to Hollywood in 1982 with the original “Blade Runner” movie, and was updated 35 years later with “Blade Runner 2049.” In Amazon Prime Video’s eight-episode streaming series, the story’s plot fast-forwards another 50 years.

Today, the idea that the lines between humans and their machines could become blurred seems less novel than it did when Dick wrote his novel. It’s so common to converse with chatbots that some have fallen in love — or have followed their advice to tragic ends.

Artificial intelligence software was recently used to solve math problems that have puzzled humans for centuries. Now humans are puzzling over the future of AI: One researcher recently left Anthropic, a leading AI company, and warned that his former colleagues were “gambling with their lives” by pursuing the technology too vigorously.

Are we coming closer to the world of “Blade Runner”? University of Washington linguist Emily M. Bender, co-author of “The AI Con,” says that would be giving AI too much credit. “There’s absolutely no reason to believe that the technological future as portrayed in ‘Blade Runner’ is even a possibility, let alone an inevitability,” she told me in the latest episode of the Fiction Science podcast.

During our podcast interview, Bender and Ryan Calo, a UW law professor specializing in the legal and policy implications of technological advances, conducted an in-depth reality check on the fictional “Blade Runner 2099” — and on the way real-world developments in the realm of AI are typically being portrayed.

Bender says the cardinal sin of AI portrayals is to make it sound as if computer programs rather than humans are responsible for what’s happening.

“When we talk about rogue agents, and agents hacking things, there’s a lot of narrative-building happening there around what’s fundamentally companies doing cyber crimes,” she says.

Calo agrees that ascribing agency to AI is problematic. “Oftentimes when you do things with or through technology, there are people present who don’t appear to be there, and I think that’s exacerbated when you give apparent agency and anthropomorphize the technology. It’s even less likely for you to see the people behind it,” he says.

But is it a crime? “As a technical matter, in order to be charged with a computer crime, like under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, you have to have some level of intent,” Calo says. “I would argue that some of these experiments are running up against recklessness.”

There’s no sign that OpenAI’s engineers intended for their AI software to hack into an Australian healthcare database in June, or Hugging Face’s computer system in July, but Calo says “they certainly are reckless as to that possibility.”

Negligence or recklessness isn’t a crime under the current terms of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. But some members of Congress favor enacting new provisions to cover recklessness.

“When you create conditions where you’re reasonably certain that some federal law is going to get broken, I’m with Emily that that should constitute a crime,” Calo says. “And it’s interesting the way that they’re avoiding responsibility — including rhetorically.”

Should governments set up agencies specifically charged with policing artificial intelligence? And if so, should the investigators be called “blade runners”? Bender doesn’t think much of that idea.

“I think if we called them ‘blade runners,’ then we are setting up what they’re investigating as not the people, but the replicants,” she says. “So, let’s keep the legal system in the real world.”

Neither Bender nor Calo favors establishing a federal agency along the lines of the Food and Drug Administration or the Federal Trade Commission specifically for artificial intelligence.

“I am always a little bit worried about the idea of an FDA for AI or something, because I don’t think that AI is one thing. That word doesn’t refer to a coherent set of technologies,” Bender says. “And I also don’t think that the required expertise is primarily expertise in the internals of these systems. It’s much more expertise in the systems that they’re impacting.”

Both researchers prefer the idea of setting up more of a “brain trust” at the federal level to help regulators at the FTC, FDA and other federal agencies understand what they’re dealing with. Bender also likes the idea of setting up a professional certification system for software engineers, while Calo has three specific suggestions for AI policy:

Revive the Office of Technology Assessment: “Congress had the confidence to intercede in technology policy because it had hundreds of nonpartisan subject-matter experts writing lengthy reports about this technology and advising them what to do,” Calo says. “It was one of the first things that Newt Gingrich got rid of during the so-called Gingrich Revolution when Republicans took over Congress in the mid-’90s. They defunded it.”

Strengthen the FTC’s regulatory role: Calo notes that the FTC’s interest in protecting consumers has waxed and waned. During the Biden administration, for example, the FTC highlighted competitive concerns about generative AI. More recently, the FTC signaled its willingness to investigate AI companies at the same time that the White House signaled its desire to reset the terms for AI regulation. The FTC is currently bound by a requirement to assess cost-benefit tradeoffs when it considers whether a trade practice is unfair, and Calo would like to see that requirement rescinded.

Protect whistleblowers and researchers: Calo would also like to see the legal system do more to protect the ability of third parties to “kick the tires” on AI tools, so that “we’re not allowing all these cease-and-desist letters … and these other pressures to try to stop accountability.”

As a linguist, Bender is particularly sensitive to the way words are used when discussing artificial intelligence. She hasn’t totally sworn off the term “AI” — after all, it’s right in the title of her book. But she’s definitely against the term “AI agent.”

“You have verbs like ‘hack’ or ‘going rogue,’ and the subject of the verb — the thing that’s doing it — is the software,” she says. “One of the functions of that is that it leaves no room in the sentence for the people who built the software and the people who use the software.”

The term “AI safety” also makes Bender uncomfortable.

“‘AI safety’ refers to the people who are concerned about not a replicant, but a Terminator — that is, people who have lost track of the fact that those are imagined characters in movies, as opposed to what’s happening in the real world,” she says. “And I think also that functions to displace concern and accountability.”

That brings us back to “Blade Runner 2099.” The new series sticks with the moody sensibility of the original movie. Yes, there are flying cars. But the technological advances are mixed in with the age-old conventions of film noir.

“In the opening scene of this new ‘Blade Runner,’ the guy is smoking a cigarette, talking about making fake people to take over a factory,” Calo says. “It’s just so wild. We have such a better capacity to imagine a technical future than we do changes in our own social norms, and I find that just fascinating.”

Bender thinks the replicants could have done a better job of cleaning up all the external wires that are dangling in the L.A. of 2099. And Calo was amazed to see so many guns being used at the brink of the 22nd century. “It’s an incredibly old and savage technology … and the fact that they’re still using them is wild,” he says.

One thing I puzzled over: The replicants don’t seem to be networked together, and they’re not instantly able to identify or locate each other wirelessly. If I were a replicant overlord, that’s the first thing I’d do.

Looking beyond the techno-nitpicking, Bender says the “Blade Runner” franchise is notable in that it doesn’t have obvious good guys and bad guys. “We don’t want to actually map the replicants onto AIs in today’s parlance, so much as mapping the replicants onto other sentient beings in our midst that maybe we don’t understand so well, and that can include other people,” she says.

The first “Blade Runner” focused on whether machines could pass as humans, but the new “Blade Runner” flips the script. Could humans pass as machines? “That has really interesting resonances with what’s happening in our current situation with technology sold as AI, because so much of it is actually repurposing the work of people,” Bender says.

Bender doesn’t believe it’s possible for “Blade Runner 2099” to become reality, but Calo isn’t quite ready to rule that out entirely. “One thing about the esthetic of ‘Blade Runner’ is, it has this apocalyptic flavor to it … and this retrograde flavor to it. I think the only way we go from 2026 to 2099 and still have that is if something horribly calamitous happens in the interim,” Calo says.

“I hope we do get a world that is more civilized than what’s being depicted,” he says. “But we’ll see.”

#5329. Cybersecurity AI startup Corma reaches $1B valuation in about 3 months

Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.

The startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP, a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled.

Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

#5328. Companies want AI-ready workers. Are they willing to adapt, too?

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 27, 2026 at 1:00 pmNovember 27, 2026 at 11:48 am

Companies want workers who can adapt to AI. Arif Gursel has a question for those employers: Are they willing to change, too?

Preparing people for technological change cannot fall entirely on students, universities or employees trying to keep their skills relevant, said Gursel, a serial entrepreneur who runs training programs in coding, AI and other fields.

“A skilled and adaptable workforce also needs a skilled and adaptable workplace. Those things have to be in balance,” he said, speaking at a recent Technology Alliance event focused on building talent in Washington state.

A study released Monday by the Schultz Family Foundation points to a related disconnect. Based on nearly 3,000 interviews with young adults, employers and others, it found that 79% of Washington businesses want new entry-level workers to have mid-level AI skills or better. Slightly less than half of the young adults surveyed felt their schooling cleared that bar.

The study didn’t examine whether employers are changing how they train workers. It did find that more than 80% of employers are interested in internships, apprenticeships and similar programs, but 77% say they lack the staff time to make that happen.

Gursel said the challenge extends to experienced workers, too. He called on employers to help design training, connect it to actual jobs and make the workplace somewhere people can develop new capabilities, rather than simply replacing those whose skills no longer match the task.

He offered an example from a past coding training program he helped build with Microsoft, a company where he worked for more than a decade early in his career. Gursel, founder of the corporate strategy firm 8genC, partnered with a Microsoft hiring manager and together they developed a curriculum and the manager committed two open positions to graduates.

Gursel argued that AI tools present an opportunity to build those kinds of partnerships again, with companies helping community colleges and nonprofits prepare people for work rather than leaving educators to guess what employers will need.

Ingrid Stegemoeller, of the Washington Roundtable’s Partnership for Learning, echoed some of those ideas in a statement about the Schultz family study.

“If we make it simpler for employers to share clear signals about the jobs and skills they need with schools, colleges and training programs, we can turn their participation into coursework and work-based learning that prepare young people for those jobs,” she said.

Coleman Bryant, a technology innovation master’s candidate at the University of Washington, also spoke on the panel. He raised concerns about AI and education: Students, he said, can end up “offloading all of the critical thinking to the AI” instead of working out solutions on their own.

He called for hands-on, interdisciplinary education that requires people to connect technical knowledge with business, design and collaboration.

The study indicated schools may be sending mixed signals on AI. About as many young adults said their institution discouraged AI use (36%) as said it helped them learn to use it (34%).

There’s also the fundamental issue of access to AI tools, Gursel said.

“There are underserved and under-resourced and marginalized communities all across Washington state, especially as we think about our tribal communities, our indigenous communities, our Black and Brown communities,” he said.

“How do we build the bridge for that digital divide that is just widening as a result of AI?” he asked.

#5327. October 22, 2019

SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed plans for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the company and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in New York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

Forty-six attorneys general have joined a New York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials announced this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the company’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

The problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into new venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” says one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she says. One venture manager who reappeared too quickly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any new relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”

SoftBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one big reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it launched a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”

#5326. Hank Green is self-funding ClockwiseTV, a curated educational video platform for kids

“I was recently on a podcast and the host asked me what my lowest part of my career was,” Hank Green mused on a recent episode of his own podcast, Dear Hank & John.

That’s a tough question for anyone to answer, let alone someone who has spent about two decades regularly posting videos online for an increasingly broad audience.

“Really the low — the long low — was just watching as [the internet] went from being this lovely thing that a bunch of creatives were goofing around [on] to it being freaking everything, and mattering so much, and getting taken over by all tons of terrible vibes and algorithms selecting for outrage, and it being a huge degradation to the social order,” Green said.

That’s bleak, but Green is at least trying to lead by example in showing that we don’t have to accept that the good parts of the internet are gone forever. The notoriously entrepreneurial vlogbrother has spun up a new company with Leslie Morgan: ClockwiseTV, a curated, ad-free educational video platform for children ages 8 to 12.

“[Hank] came to me last September like, ‘I have had this idea for a really long time, and it stems from the fact that my child, who’s nine, always is asking me for five more minutes on whatever device he’s on,’” Morgan, who has spent 20 years working on the business side of the creator economy, told TechCrunch. “I was like, I have that same problem… ‘How do you contain time, but also give the child agency?’”

Clockwise’s answer to that question seems to be this: At the start of each viewing session, the parent and child decide how long they can watch, and the platform will recommend videos that will adhere to that time frame. If a kid is in the midst of a 30-minute session and has already watched two 10-minute videos, they’re not going to be suggested a 20-minute video when they only have 10 minutes left.

The startup is addressing a pretty widespread concern among parents, who are worried about more than simply negotiating with their children about how long they can use the iPad. According to a 2025 study by the Pew Research Center, about 51% of parents of children 12 or younger say their kid watches YouTube every day, among other video apps.

YouTube has a dedicated app for children under 13, YouTube Kids, which offers a wide range of parental controls, but the app can reportedly still serve children a wealth of low-quality AI slop. Other apps that don’t have a kids’ version can be even worse.

Clockwise says it is also solving that problem by hand-curating a library of educational videos from creators like Odd Animal Specimens, Draw with Jazza, and Nerdforge, as well as channels Green had a hand in creating, like Crash Course Kids and SciShow Kids.

“When you go into the app, there’s a dozen choices [of videos] that you can choose from to start,” Morgan, the startup’s CEO, said. “There’s search functionality as well, so you can say, ‘Hey, I’m really interested in math today,’ so you can look up Stand-up Maths and look at what’s available in that time frame.”

Some of these creators cater to people of all ages, but Clockwise says its team manually reviews each video it uploads and edits it so that it’s ready for younger eyes. The team might remove anything from embedded product placement to what Morgan calls “spectacle power tool use.”

“Simone Giertz, who’s a maker creator, tends to curse a lot. But a lot of that content is great for kids,” Morgan explains. “She makes a skateboard for her three-legged dog, and if she drops an f-bomb, we’re going to cut it out so that it’s suitable for children.”

Clockwise pays these creators an upfront fee to use their videos, then shares 25% of revenue based on watch time. Clockwise charges parents $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year to access the platform, which it promises will remain free of ads.

“Humans are checking [the videos] four times at least before it’s ever published into our app […] That will always stay,” Morgan said. “We’re not interested in using AI to wash down our content.”

So far, a few hundred parents have tested Clockwise with their children in beta. On Tuesday, the platform is opening to the public with apps made for iOS and Android smartphones and tablets.

The platform has not taken on any outside funding, and is funded by Green himself.

“It was really important that he had full control,” Morgan said. “He wanted to invest his own wealth into this. That was also really important because it is something he just believes in so wholeheartedly, as do I.”

#5325. Amazon discriminated against Iranian job candidate under global hiring policy, Ontario tribunal rules

by Todd Bishop on Nov 27, 2026 at 2:21 pmNovember 27, 2026 at 2:21 pm

An Ontario human rights tribunal ruled that Amazon violated provincial law when it dropped a Toronto software engineer from its hiring process because of his Iranian citizenship.

The company’s internal policy, applied worldwide, barred some Iranian citizens from jobs involving access to Amazon’s encrypted technology, according to the ruling.

In a Nov. 16 decision, the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario ordered Amazon to pay 15,000 Canadian dollars (about US$10,500) plus interest to Mohammadhasan Owlia, whose hiring process it ended in 2020. The tribunal rejected Amazon’s argument that U.S. export controls required the policy.

Export controls are U.S. rules that limit who can get access to certain American technology, including some encryption software.

The tribunal found that Amazon never showed that the mid-level software engineering job for which Owlia applied would have involved any restricted technology. Expert witnesses for both sides agreed that the U.S. rules don’t ban hiring Iranian citizens, though a company may need a government license before giving them access to certain technology.

“Stated simply, Amazon’s export controls compliance policy was overbroad,” wrote Cyndee Todgham Cherniak, the tribunal vice-chair who decided the case.

Amazon said in a statement to Canadian news outlets that it is committed to “fair and inclusive hiring and to following the laws wherever we operate, including Ontario’s Human Rights Code,” and that it will review the decision and meet its obligations under it.

The ruling was reported earlier by the Toronto Star and the Globe and Mail. We’ve asked Amazon whether the policy remains in effect elsewhere, including in the U.S.

Owlia, a University of Toronto engineering graduate who held an open work permit allowing him to work in Canada, applied for the job in 2019 and passed Amazon’s online technical assessment. On a pre-interview call in January 2020, a recruiter noticed he had studied in Tehran and told him Amazon had a policy against hiring Iranians.

Amazon’s guide for recruiters, quoted in the decision, says to end the process in those cases and tell candidates only that the company “has decided to not move forward with the hiring process.”

The policy, as quoted in the decision, also covers citizens of Cuba, North Korea, Sudan and Syria. It covers candidates, employees, temporary workers and contractors with access to Amazon’s encrypted technology, except lower-level warehouse jobs. It applies globally, but it exempts U.S. citizens, U.S. permanent residents, refugees, people granted asylum, and anyone whose most recent citizenship or permanent residency is from a country not on the list.

Owlia’s lawyers noted that an Amazon recruitment manager acknowledged during cross-examination that the policy remained in effect, according to the ruling. She also testified that Owlia would have been eligible once he became a Canadian permanent resident in 2021.

The tribunal’s orders apply only to hiring in Ontario by Amazon Fulfillment Services ULC, the Canadian subsidiary named in the case. Within six months, Amazon must revise the policy and the recruiter guide to require compliance with Ontario’s Human Rights Code there, and its Ontario-based HR staff must take human rights training.

The tribunal declined to award about C$92,500 (about US$65,000) in lost wages, calling the claim too speculative.

“In my view, having to comply with multiple laws is a cost of doing business,” Todgham Cherniak wrote.

In the U.S., the Immigration and Nationality Act protects U.S. citizens and nationals, eligible permanent residents, refugees and people granted asylum from hiring discrimination based on citizenship status. Workers on temporary visas generally fall outside that specific protection. The Justice Department has warned employers that screening out applicants from particular countries can still amount to national origin discrimination.

The U.S. Commerce Department says that giving Iranian nationals access to controlled technology or certain software can require a license, including when the transfer happens in the U.S. or a third country.

A similar dispute surfaced at Booking.com in 2022, when the company canceled the employment contracts of 11 Iranian hires living in Iran just before they were due to start at its Amsterdam headquarters. Booking.com cited complications in hiring and relocating them and said the move had nothing to do with discrimination, Skift reported. An internal document cited a possible “sanction risk” in employing Iranian residents, according to NL Times.

“I’m proud that I stood up for my right to be judged on my ability to do the work, instead of where my birth certificate was issued,” Owlia said in a statement released by his lawyers at Toronto firm Kastner Ko.

Owlia is now a Canadian citizen and an engineering manager at a Toronto software startup.

A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing company was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

The CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

It happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics company to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.)

In a higher-profile case, James Damore, the fired Google engineer who authored that infamous memo about the company’s diversity practices and whose LinkedIn page cited under “Education” a “PhD, Systems Biology,” removed mention of those doctoral studies after Wired confirmed with Harvard that he was enrolled in the program but didn’t complete the doctorate.

Damore tried to defend his own LinkedIn profile, tweeting at the time, “I never told anyone I have a PhD. LinkedIn can’t distinguish between being in the PhD program and having a PhD (I forgot to update it).”

#5323. Why Is Crypto Up Today? BTC Back Above $60K – is the Bull Market Back?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Why Is Crypto Up Today? This is the question every trader is asking after the cryptocurrency market staged a clear rebound on Thursday, November 26, 2026, snapping a multi-day losing streak and giving battered traders some relief.

After sliding to multi-week lows earlier in the week, major tokens climbed as buyers stepped in at discounted levels. The total market cap is up over +2% overnight, sitting at $2.15 trillion, with Bitcoin crucially reclaiming $60K with a near-4% daily move.

Bitcoin reclaimed the psychologically important $60,000 level and traded between roughly $60,400 and $60,800, gaining about 2.5–3% over 24 hours. Ethereum followed closely, rising to the $1,690–$1,700 range for a similar percentage gain.

Solana outperformed, advancing roughly 4% to $70.50–$71.20, while XRP climbed about 3.5–4.5% to $0.95–$0.96. The total crypto market capitalization recovered to approximately $2.10–$2.16 trillion, up 1–2% on the day according to CoinGecko data.

Trading volume remained elevated, up 22% from yesterday to $86.4Bn, and short liquidations added upward pressure as overleveraged bearish positions were forced to cover.

Several factors combined to fuel the bounce. First, prices had become deeply oversold after Bitcoin’s drop toward the $57,000–$58,000 zone. Technical indicators such as RSI on shorter timeframes reached extreme low readings, historically a setup that attracts dip-buyers and algorithmic mean-reversion trades.

Second, equity markets provided a supportive backdrop. A recovery in technology and AI-related stocks helped lift risk appetite more broadly, and crypto continues to trade with a high correlation to those sectors.

Positive developments around a U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill clearing a House committee also offered a modest sentiment boost, reminding investors that longer-term institutional and policy interest has not disappeared.

Even as U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs continued to post outflows (including a sizable figure on the prior session), the market rose anyway. This divergence often signals that stronger hands are absorbing remaining sellers or that short covering is outweighing institutional redemptions in the short term.

BIG REVERSAL IN THE MARKET$2.7 TRILLION has been added back to U.S. stocks, crypto, and precious metals in the last 2 hours. pic.twitter.com/Xg6ug97Pce

Explore: The Best Token Presales Right Now

The most encouraging aspect of today’s move is that it occurred after an extended period of heavy selling and extreme fear. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index remained in Extreme Fear territory (readings near 11–13 as of November 26).

This is a level that has frequently coincided with local bottoms in previous cycles. When the market can rally while sentiment is still this depressed, it often suggests forced selling is exhausting, and patient capital is beginning to accumulate.

Bitcoin’s ability to reclaim and hold above $60,000 after testing lower support is particularly constructive. A series of higher lows on the daily chart, if sustained, would mark a potential shift in short-term market structure.

While one day of gains does not confirm a new bull market, the conditions for a more sustained recovery are starting to align. Extreme fear, oversold technicals, and visible dip-buying create a classic setup for multi-week or multi-month advances once the selling pressure fully abates.

If ETF outflows begin to slow or reverse in the coming sessions, and if upcoming economic data softens rate-hike expectations, the path higher would open more clearly.

Institutional accumulation has continued in the background even during the recent drawdown, and any improvement in broader risk sentiment could amplify the move. For now, today’s rebound offers the first tangible evidence in days that the worst of the immediate selling may be behind the market.

Whether it becomes a durable rally will depend on follow-through volume and Bitcoin’s ability to defend the $60,000 area, but the green candles offer a welcome dose of hope to those eagerly wondering why crypto is up today.

#5322. Science Corporation’s brain tech is worth $3.5 billion after new funding

Science Corporation, the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the company said in a blog post.

Investors in the new round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for new conditions.

Hodak announced that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

With the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.

Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The company is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

#5320. Pedestal AI raises $4.7 million to agentify the supply chain

Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly.

On Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding. The company’s goal is to use agentic AI to make supply chains faster and more reliable — a plan that’s already brought them together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world.

The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage. Pedestal says the funding will be used to expand its product and engineering time, grow the marketing organization, and support additional deployments.

In practice, much of Pedestal’s work is about removing friction from the shipping process — with agentic technology used as a means to that end. In one case, the company reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work that drivers were supposed to do. The agentic system they built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions; if the call didn’t go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. Along the way, the deployment collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which could be used to optimize the system even further.

CEO Raj Aggarwal says contemporary AI systems are particularly useful for dealing with that data. “The challenge is that the data is messy and it’s constantly changing,” Aggarwal told TechCrunch. “It’s disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. That’s what makes it hard.”

Supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups. The supply chain startup Atomic, launched by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory. Another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics.

As Aggarwal sees it, deliveries are particularly well-suited to training reinforcement learning systems. Because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, it’s easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what’s working and away from what isn’t.

Perhaps most importantly, it’s the kind of problem that can have an immediate effect on a client’s bottom line, making it easy to justify the expense.

“If you can get it right,” he told TechCrunch, “you can have really big impact.”

#5319. October 25, 2019

And it’s Friday! [Throws frisbee into tree.]

Before we dive into the newsletter, one more bit of great news about our upcoming event (which we promise we’ll stop talking about soon): Michael Grimes, the star tech banker from Morgan Stanley at the center of Uber’s IPO (and Facebook IPO, and Slack’s and Spotify’s), has been persuaded to come and talk about direct listings, which we’re very excited about. If you’re as confused as we are about whether these make sense for more than a couple of companies each year (current status: we don’t think they do), you won’t want to miss this rare conversation with “Wall Street’s Silicon Valley whisperer.”

Note that seats are almost gone. Giant thanks to NextWorld, the early-stage enterprise-focused firm that’s hosting all of us; to KCPR, the boutique tech PR and strategy firm; and to Carta, a platform that helps companies and VCs manage their cap tables, valuations, investments, and equity plans, for their support.

Ben Horowitz,  the co-founder of the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, has a new book coming out this coming Monday titled “What You Do is Who You Are,” that takes a look at how to create “culture” at a company.

It’s a word that’s thrown around a lot but that’s very hard to grasp, let alone implement in a sustainable way. Horowitz learned firsthand as a CEO how elusive it can be when he took stock of his company, only to discover it was made up of “screamers who intimidated their people,” others who “neglected to give any feedback,” and at least one compulsive liar who excelled at sucking up to Horowitz and also making up stories from whole cloth.

Horowitz says creating culture was a missing part of his education, and in this new book — a follow-up to his best-selling “The Hard Thing About Hard Things” — he does his best to fill that gap for other CEOs, using his own experience, as well as lessons gleaned from historical figures Toussaint Louverture and Genghis Khan, along with Shaka Senghor, a contemporary who served time for murder and today is a criminal justice reform advocate.

It’s an instructive and novel combination, and we suggest picking up the book, especially if you love history. In the meantime, we sat down recently with Horowitz to talk about its timing and whether some of the biggest cultural blow-ups in the startup industry — Uber and WeWork — could have been avoided. These excerpts have been edited for length and clarity. Note that we’ll have more of the conversation — including Horowitz’s thoughts about dual-class shares —  for readers of Extra Crunch on Monday.

You’ve just written a book about culture that’s coming out just as a lot of questions are being raised about culture because of WeWork. What happened there?

[Cofounder Adam Neumann] had a certain kind of culture there. He had some holes — some great strengths and great holes. And sometimes that happens. When you’re really good at part of it, you can delude yourself into thinking that you’ve got everything you need when you have some massive incompleteness.

Adam is so amazing. Like, the way they got all the money and everything. And the vision was so spectacular. And everybody there believed it, and they recruited some phenomenal talent. But when you’re that optimistic, it does help to have something in the culture that says [allows] people to bring you the bad news, like, if the accounting is all over the place or what have you.

As with Uber’s Travis Kalanick, whose culture also came under fire, Neumann operated in very plain sight. He wasn’t hiding who he was or what he was spending.

Right, everybody knew how Travis was running the company. Everyone in Silicon Valley knew, let alone everyone on the board. The culture was published. You can look up Uber’s values [from that period].

Travis designed, I think, a really compelling culture, and believed in it, and published it. And the consequences of what he was missing were also super well-known. It’s only when board members think people are coming after them that [they take an interest in these things].

What are the biggest lessons in these two cases?

I obviously know more about Uber [as a Lyft investor who follows the space]. In Uber’s case, it’s a very subtle thing. Travis had a really good code. But he had a bug in it.

I think it was reported that, like, Travis encouraged bad behavior. I don’t think he did at all. I just think he didn’t make it clear that legal and ethical [considerations] were more important than competitiveness. As a result, when left to their own devices, in a distributed organization where there was a lot of distributed power, that combination had people doing things that were out of bounds.

And he was making everybody so much money. And the company was growing so fast that, for the board members, I suspect they were like, ‘As long as it’s making money, I’m not going to worry about what happens next.’

To me, the unfair part is, like, they shouldn’t get any credit at the end. Whatever you’re blaming Travis for [you should blame them, too] because they didn’t see it, either. I think that’s a charitable way of putting it.
